notes.title: The CPython Execution Model

headings.text: Walk me through everything that happens between saving a .py file and a line of it running.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Execution model — Language reference: execution model

  • dis — dis — disassembler for Python bytecode

  • Import and __pycache__ — Compiled Python files

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — GeeksforGeeks: Understanding the execution of a Python program

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

"Is Python compiled or interpreted?" is asked in almost every screen, and both one-word answers are wrong in a way the interviewer is specifically listening for. The trap is that the honest answer has two stages in it, and people who only know one of them cannot explain where __pycache__ came from or why dis exists.

2. What Python normally does

Run a file and Python appears to execute your source directly. It does not — and the evidence is sitting in your project directory:

myproject/
├── main.py
└── __pycache__/
    └── helpers.cpython-312.pyc      ← nobody asked for this

That file is bytecode, and it is there because CPython compiled helpers.py before running any of it. You can look at the same output for any function without going near the filesystem:

>>> import dis
>>> def add(a, b):
...     return a + b
...
>>> dis.dis(add)
  2     LOAD_FAST    0 (a)
        LOAD_FAST    1 (b)
        BINARY_OP    0 (+)
        RETURN_VALUE

Those are not CPU instructions. They are instructions for a stack machine that lives inside CPython, and the pipeline that produced them runs every time a module is first imported:

  .py source
      ↓   lexing + parsing
     AST
      ↓   compilation
   bytecode  ──→ cached as __pycache__/<mod>.cpython-XY.pyc
      ↓
  evaluation loop (the "PVM")   ← reads one instruction at a time
      ↓
  C code in the interpreter, then the OS

So both halves of the question are true, in sequence. There is a real compile step, and it produces bytecode rather than machine code; then there is a real interpreter, executing that bytecode instruction by instruction.

The accurate sentence is: CPython is a bytecode-compiled, interpreted runtime — compiled ahead of execution, never ahead of time to native code.

3. What changes

Two consequences follow, and they are what the question is actually probing.

The first is cost. Because there is no native-code step, every bytecode instruction is a trip through the evaluation loop — decode, dispatch, manipulate the stack — and that per-instruction overhead is the floor under Python's single-threaded speed. It is why a tight numeric loop in pure Python is orders of magnitude slower than the same loop in C, and why the standard fix is not "optimise the loop" but "do the loop somewhere else": NumPy, a C extension, or Cython, all of which move the iteration out of the evaluation loop entirely.

The second is what the instructions operate on. Everything is a heap-allocated object with a type pointer and a reference count, and a name is a slot holding a pointer to one:

    x = 10

    frame locals                 heap
      "x" ──────────────────→  ┌──────────────────┐
                               │ int object       │
                               │ value: 10        │
                               │ refcount: 1      │
                               │ type: <class int>│
                               └──────────────────┘

There are no primitives, so 10 is an object, add is an object, int is an object, and the module itself is an object. That uniformity is what buys you introspection, first-class functions, decorators and monkey-patching — and it is also what costs you the boxing overhead that makes a list of a million ints so much larger than an array of a million ints.

The trade in one sentence: Python gives up native-code speed and unboxed data, and gets back a uniform object model you can inspect and rewrite at runtime.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Three stages deserve a sentence each, because each is a separate follow-up question.

Caching is per-module and version-tagged. Only imported modules get a .pyc; the script you invoke directly is compiled in memory and thrown away. The filename carries the interpreter version (cpython-312) because bytecode is not stable across releases, and CPython checks the source's mtime and size before reusing a cached file — which is why editing a module invalidates its cache automatically, and why shipping .pyc files without their sources is a deployment choice with real caveats.

The evaluation loop is where the frames live. Each call pushes a frame holding the fast-locals array, the value stack and the instruction pointer; each return pops it. That is the same structure a traceback prints, and the same structure a generator keeps alive when it suspends rather than discarding.

Memory is refcounting first, GC second. Every object carries a count that rises on binding and falls on rebinding or scope exit, and reaching zero frees it immediately — which is why CPython's memory behaviour is so predictable compared to a tracing-GC language. The cyclic collector exists only to catch reference cycles that refcounting alone can never free.

One comparison is worth holding for the "is it slow?" follow-up. PyPy replaces the evaluation loop with a tracing JIT that compiles hot paths to native code, which is why it can be dramatically faster on long-running pure-Python loops and no faster at all on short scripts or on code that spends its time inside C extensions. CPython remains the reference implementation, and the one whose implementation details — refcounting, the GIL, the object layout — every other topic in this vault is describing.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
import dis, sys

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

dis.dis(add)                    # LOAD_FAST a; LOAD_FAST b; BINARY_OP +; RETURN_VALUE
print(add.__code__.co_consts)   # the constants table baked in at compile time
print(sys.implementation.name, sys.version_info[:2])   # ('cpython', (3, 12))

# frames are real objects you can inspect — this is what a traceback walks
def outer():
    return sys._getframe().f_code.co_name, sys._getframe(1).f_code.co_name
print(outer())                  # ('outer', '<module>')

The co_consts line is the one worth remembering for interviews: it proves the compile step happened, because the literals in your function body are already extracted into a table before anything runs. Opcode names have moved across releases — BINARY_ADD became BINARY_OP in 3.11 — so disassemble on your own interpreter rather than quoting a listing from memory.

7. The deeper mental model

Every runtime question about Python resolves to the same two-layer picture:

   your code                     what it becomes

   source text        ──→   bytecode         "what to do"
                                 ↓
   the interpreter    ──→   eval loop        "who does it"
                                 ↓
   your data          ──→   heap PyObjects   "what it does it to"
                                 ↓
                            refcount + GC    "who cleans up"

The GIL is a lock protecting that shared heap. Reference counting is the third row's bookkeeping. __slots__ is a change to the third row's layout. Generators are the eval loop keeping a frame instead of dropping it. Asyncio is one thread driving that loop between suspended frames. None of those are separate systems — they are all consequences of a design where code becomes bytecode, one interpreter executes it, and every value is a counted object on a shared heap.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Compiled or interpreted? Both, in sequence: compiled to bytecode, then that bytecode is interpreted.
What is in __pycache__? Cached bytecode for imported modules, tagged with the interpreter version.
Why is pure-Python looping slow? Per-instruction evaluation-loop overhead; there is no native-code step.
CPython vs PyPy in one line? CPython interprets bytecode with refcounting; PyPy JIT-compiles hot paths to native code.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. This is the one that gets asked verbatim — rehearse it until it runs about twenty seconds cleanly.

Tier 1 — Verifier

Is Python compiled or interpreted?

Both, and the order matters. CPython first compiles your source into bytecode — a compact intermediate instruction set, not machine code — and then a stack-based evaluation loop interprets that bytecode one instruction at a time. For imported modules the bytecode is cached in __pycache__ as a version-tagged .pyc so the compile step is skipped next time.

So the precise phrasing is that CPython is a bytecode-compiled, interpreted runtime. There is no ahead-of-time step to native code, which is exactly where Python's per-instruction interpreter overhead comes from — and it is why the standard performance answer is to move hot loops out of the evaluation loop into C, rather than to micro-optimise the Python.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Walk me through everything that happens between saving a .py file and a line of it running.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name the stages — and whether you know that the .pyc is a cache rather than a required artefact.

The source is lexed and parsed into an AST, and the compiler walks that AST to emit bytecode along with a constants table and the local-variable layout, all packaged into a code object. If this is an imported module, CPython writes that bytecode to __pycache__/<mod>.cpython-XY.pyc, tagged with the interpreter version because bytecode is not stable across releases; on the next import it validates the cache against the source's mtime and size and reuses it if they match. A script run directly as __main__ is compiled in memory and never cached.

Execution then happens in the evaluation loop. Calling a function pushes a frame holding the fast-locals array, the value stack and the instruction pointer, and the loop decodes and dispatches one opcode at a time against that frame — which is the same frame structure a traceback prints and a generator retains when it suspends. Everything those opcodes touch is a heap-allocated object with a type pointer and a reference count; binding a name increments the count, rebinding or leaving scope decrements it, and hitting zero frees the object immediately, with the generational cyclic collector existing only to reclaim reference cycles that refcounting alone cannot.

10. Quick Comparison Table

CPython PyPy
Execution bytecode interpreted by the eval loop tracing JIT compiles hot paths to native code
Best case the reference for correctness and C-API compatibility long-running pure-Python loops
Worst case tight numeric loops in pure Python short scripts; code dominated by C extensions
Memory management reference counting + generational cyclic GC tracing GC, no refcounting
C extension story the C API is native to it works via cpyext, with a compatibility and speed cost

11. What Goes Wrong

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Python is an interpreted language — it executes the source line by line."

✅ Reality: The whole module is compiled to bytecode first, and the interpreter executes that. Saying "line by line" is what invites the follow-up about __pycache__ that you then cannot answer.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Python always runs the .pyc file."

✅ Reality: The .pyc is a cache for imported modules only, validated against the source's mtime and size. A script run directly is compiled in memory and never written out.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

"Compiled versus interpreted" is not a property of a language, it is a property of an implementation — which is why the same Python source runs under CPython's interpreter, PyPy's JIT and, historically, Jython on the JVM. Separately, bytecode is not machine code: it is an instruction set for CPython's own stack machine, which is precisely why .pyc files are version-tagged and not portable across releases.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't answer "interpreted" and stop — it is the answer that ends the conversation badly, because the next question is always about bytecode or __pycache__.

  • Don't quote specific opcode names from memory — they change between releases (BINARY_ADD → BINARY_OP in 3.11, plus the specialising adaptive interpreter's internal opcodes). Disassemble on the version you are describing.

  • Don't reach for PyPy as a general performance answer — it helps long-running pure-Python hot loops and hurts on short processes and C-extension-heavy stacks, which describes most web and data workloads.

  • Don't treat shipping .pyc without sources as obfuscation — it is trivially decompilable, and it ties the artefact to one interpreter version.

🔖 Version discipline

Bytecode and opcode names are explicitly not a stable interface, and they have moved substantially across 3.11–3.13 with the specialising adaptive interpreter, so anything opcode-level must be stated against a version and re-checked with dis. The __pycache__ layout and the cpython-XY tag have been stable since 3.2. Free-threaded builds (3.13+, PEP 703) change the memory and refcounting story materially and are the thing most likely to date this note — verify before asserting how refcounting behaves under threads.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • None — this is the foundation the rest of the CPython material is built on. Read it first.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • Names, binding and assignment — what the STORE_FAST in that disassembly actually does.

  • Reference counting and the cyclic GC — the third row of the mental model, in detail.

  • The GIL and concurrency — the lock that exists because that heap is shared.

  • Generators and asyncio — the evaluation loop retaining frames instead of dropping them.

15. Lock it in

CPython compiles source to bytecode, then interprets the bytecode.
Compiled ahead of execution — never ahead of time to native code.

notes.title: Names, Binding & Assignment

headings.text: Walk me through what the interpreter actually does when it executes b = a.
A caller passes a config dict into a helper that "tweaks a couple of defaults", and later requests see corrupted config. What happened?

You're designing a request-scoped context object passed through a chain of async handlers. Mutation-through-alias has already caused one production incident. How do you design its binding semantics to prevent a repeat?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Naming & binding — Execution model: naming and binding

  • Assignment statements — Language reference: assignment statements

  • Augmented assignment — Language reference: augmented assignment statements

  • Bonus — Ned Batchelder: Facts and myths about Python names and values

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: Variables in Python

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

Almost everyone arrives at Python from a language where a variable is a box: you declare it, the compiler reserves some bytes, and assigning puts a value into those bytes. Python looks exactly like that from the outside, right up until the day a function you called "just reads the config" quietly corrupts it for every later request.

The problem this solves is the one you hit the moment you have two names for the same thing and you cannot predict which changes travel between them. It shows up as a helper that mutates its argument, a class default that accumulates across instances, a cached dict that "randomly" changes shape.

So carry one question through this note: when you write b = a, what exactly got written where? Not conceptually — literally. Once you can answer that in one sentence, every aliasing bug you have ever seen collapses into the same bug.

2. What Python normally does

Start with two lines you have written a thousand times.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a

Ask the box question: did Python just reserve room for a second list? It did not, and you can prove it without reading a single word of documentation:

>>> id(a) == id(b)
True

id() reports the object's identity — in CPython, its address. Two names, one address, which means one list. The second line did not build anything. It took the pointer already sitting in a's slot and wrote that same pointer into b's slot.

That is the whole default, and it is worth stating in the shape of a picture, because the picture is what makes the rest of the note obvious. A name is not the thing. A name is an entry in a namespace holding a pointer to a thing:

namespace (function locals / module dict)
 ├── "a" ──┐
 │         ├──→ ┌───────────────┐
 └── "b" ──┘    │ list object   │
                │ [1, 2, 3]     │
                │ refcount: 2   │
                └───────────────┘

Two arrows, one box. And because binding is just a pointer write, it costs the same whether the object is a three-element list or a 400 MB DataFrame — you are copying one machine word, never the payload.

Now the behaviour this default makes possible, the one you have relied on without noticing. Because both names reach the same object, a change made through one is a change seen through the other:

>>> b.append(4)
>>> a
[1, 2, 3, 4]

You never touched a. You did not have to — there was only ever one list, and a is just another way of reaching it.

So by default assignment shares, it never copies, and every name bound to an object is a live window onto it.

3. What changes

Here is where the model people carry in starts to break, because the very next line looks like more of the same and behaves completely differently.

b = b + [5]

Same variable, same list, another element added — and yet:

>>> a
[1, 2, 3, 4]
>>> b
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> id(a) == id(b)
False

a did not move. The two names have come apart. And the reason is the distinction this whole topic exists to install: b.append(4) mutated the object; b = b + [5] rebound the name.

Mutation reaches through the name to the object and changes it, so everyone pointing at that object sees the change. Rebinding never touches the object at all. It builds a new one, then overwrites the pointer in one namespace slot — and every other name carries on pointing exactly where it was.

Put the two side by side and the difference is spatial rather than verbal:

MUTATION  b.append(4)        REBINDING  b = b + [5]

 "a" ──┐                      "a" ──→ [1,2,3,4]     (untouched)
       ├──→ [1,2,3,4]
 "b" ──┘                      "b" ──→ [1,2,3,4,5]   (new object)

 one object, changed          two objects, one pointer moved

This is also the honest answer to the interview question about argument passing, and it is why neither of the usual labels fits. Pass a list into a function and the function gets its own local name bound to your object:

def sneaky(lst):
    lst.append(99)      # mutation — reaches your object
    lst = []            # rebinding — repoints the local name only
    return lst

mine = [1]
sneaky(mine)

>>> mine
[1, 99]

The append landed on your list. The lst = [] did not, because it only overwrote the function's local slot, which disappeared the moment the function returned. Pass-by-reference would have let that lst = [] clear your variable; pass-by-value would have stopped the append from reaching you. Python does neither, which is why the precise name is pass-by-object-reference, or call-by-sharing.

The trade in one sentence: Python gives you O(1) assignment and free sharing of arbitrarily large objects, and in exchange you must decide, deliberately, at every boundary, whether you meant to share.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Conceptually, a name is a label and assignment moves the label. In CPython the implementation is narrower than that and worth knowing precisely, because it explains the costs.

A name is a slot. Inside a function it is a numbered entry in the frame's fast-locals array, fixed at compile time; at module or class level it is a key in a real dictionary. Assignment writes a PyObject * into that slot and adjusts reference counts. Disassemble the statement and there is nothing else in it:

>>> import dis
>>> dis.dis(compile("b = a", "<s>", "exec"))
  1           LOAD_NAME    0 (a)
              STORE_NAME   1 (b)

LOAD_NAME pushes the pointer already held in a onto the evaluation stack; STORE_NAME pops it into b. Two instructions, one pointer, no constructor call anywhere.

Read the two paths and every behaviour above falls out. On the left, nothing is constructed, so identity is shared and the refcount rises — which is also why the object outlives del a, since b is still holding it up. On the right, the expression is evaluated first and produces a genuinely new object, so the store lands on a different pointer and the two names diverge from that instruction onward.

One stage deserves its own sentence because it is the piece people miss. The object is never consulted about the assignment. STORE_FAST does not call a method on the list, does not ask the type whether it wants to be shared, and has no idea the object is aliased. That is why aliasing is invisible at the call site and why no amount of care inside a class can protect it from being shared — the sharing happens in the caller's namespace, not in the object.

The one place that invariant bends is augmented assignment, and it bends in a way that is exam material. b += [5] compiles to a BINARY_OP with an in-place flag, which gives the type a chance to answer via __iadd__. A list implements it, mutates itself, and returns itself — so the store writes back the same pointer and aliases see the change. An int implements no such thing, so Python falls back to __add__, gets a new object, and stores that. Identical syntax, opposite semantics, decided entirely by whether the type is mutable.

5. Code / Config Example

The production shape of this is a boundary: something arrives from outside and you have to decide whether to share it or own it. Getting that decision wrong is the bug this note prevents.

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace, field

DEFAULTS = {"timeout": 30, "retries": 3}        # module-level: shared by everyone

def make_config(overrides: dict) -> dict:
    cfg = dict(DEFAULTS)                        # explicit copy AT the boundary;
    cfg.update(overrides)                       # without it, update() writes
    return cfg                                  # straight into DEFAULTS forever

@dataclass(frozen=True)                         # the structural fix: rebinding
class RequestCtx:                               # is the ONLY way to "change" it
    user_id: str
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()                  # tuple, not list — no mutable
                                                # field can be aliased out
def with_user(ctx: RequestCtx, uid: str) -> RequestCtx:
    return replace(ctx, user_id=uid)            # returns a NEW ctx; callers
                                                # upstream keep the old binding

Two different tools for the same hazard. make_config keeps the mutable dict but pays one explicit copy so that update() can only ever touch an object this function owns. RequestCtx removes the hazard structurally: there is nothing to mutate, so a handler that wants a change must rebind its own local name and hand the new object forward. Reach for the first when the object is small and short-lived, the second when the object is threaded through code you do not control.

6. Break it yourself

Paste this into a REPL. It runs the same += against a mutable type and an immutable one and prints the object's identity on either side, which is the only way to see the difference rather than be told about it.

xs = [1]
ys = xs
before = id(xs)
xs += [2]                     # list: __iadd__ mutates in place
print(id(xs) == before, ys)   # ?

n = 1
m = n
before = id(n)
n += 1                        # int: no __iadd__, falls back to __add__
print(id(n) == before, m)     # ?

# what to look for: line 1 keeps its identity and ys sees [1, 2]; line 2 gets a
#                   new identity and m is still 1
# naive model would predict: both print the same thing, because += is just x = x + y

You get True [1, 2] and then False 1. The list kept its address and its alias saw the new element; the int got a fresh address and its alias saw nothing.

What that proves is that += has no fixed meaning. It is a request, and the type answers it — mutate-and-return-self for a list, build-a-new-one for an int. So the question "does this line affect my caller?" can never be answered from the syntax alone. You have to know the type, and that is precisely why the mutable-default and shared-config bugs keep getting through review: the buggy line looks identical to the safe one.

7. The deeper mental model

Zoom out and the specific rule turns out to be one layer of something the language does everywhere:

        Python's actual shape              What you were picturing

   namespace                               variable
       ↓                                       ↓
   "name" → pointer                       bytes in a box
       ↓                                       ↓
   heap object (type, refcount, value)    the value itself
       ↓
   reached by every name bound to it      reached by one variable

Everything in Python lives in the third row and is only ever reached indirectly. Functions, classes, modules and instances are all just objects on the heap, and def, class and import are all binding statements — def f(): ... builds a function object and binds the name f to it, no differently from f = lambda: .... That is why you can put a function in a dict, why a decorator is only f = decorator(f) written sideways, and why monkey-patching works at all.

The second row is the one that varies. Names in a function are compiled to array slots; names at module level are dictionary keys; attribute names are keys in an instance __dict__; slotted attributes are fixed offsets. Different storage, same relationship — a name is a reference to an object, never the object itself.

So the thing to carry away is not "Python doesn't copy." It is that Python has exactly one kind of variable, and the question of who else can see your change is always a question about how many names reached that object, never about what the assignment looked like.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is a Python variable, mechanically? A namespace slot holding a pointer to a heap object — not a box holding bytes.
Does b = a ever copy the object? Never. It writes the same pointer into a second slot; id(a) == id(b).
Rebinding vs mutation? Rebinding repoints one name; mutation changes the shared object and every name sees it.
What does "pass-by-object-reference" mean? The reference is copied by value into the parameter; caller and callee share the object.
Why does x += 1 on an int not affect an alias? No __iadd__ on int, so it falls back to __add__ and rebinds to a new object.
What bytecode does b = a emit? LOAD_FAST a then STORE_FAST b — a pointer push and a pointer store.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Skipped — the Section 4 diagram illustrates a two-instruction sequence rather than a structure you must reconstruct. The load-bearing picture here is the two-names-one-object sketch in Section 2, which is already a recall aid.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you get before the follow-up lands. Everything below Tier 1 is what they follow up with.

Tier 1 — Verifier

Is Python pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

Neither label fits, and the precise term is pass-by-object-reference — sometimes called call-by-sharing. When you pass an argument, Python copies the reference into the parameter name by value, so caller and callee hold two names for one object.

That gives you the behaviour interviewers are actually checking for: mutating the object through the parameter is visible to the caller, because it is their object; rebinding the parameter is not, because rebinding only overwrites the function's local slot.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Walk me through what the interpreter actually does when it executes b = a.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name namespace slots and refcounts, or only paraphrase "it points at the same thing".

The right-hand side is evaluated to a reference to an existing object: LOAD_FAST a pushes the pointer held in a's slot onto the evaluation stack. Then STORE_FAST b pops it and writes it into b's slot, incrementing the object's reference count. Nothing is constructed and no fields are copied — inside a function those slots are numbered entries in the frame's fast-locals array, fixed at compile time; at module level they are keys in the module __dict__.

Two things follow. Binding is O(1) regardless of object size, because you are copying one machine word rather than the payload. And the refcount increment is what ties binding to object lifetime: the object survives del a because b is still holding it up, and it is freed at whichever rebind or scope exit drops the count to zero. The object itself is never consulted during any of this, which is exactly why aliasing is invisible at the call site.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A caller passes a config dict into a helper that "tweaks a couple of defaults", and later requests see corrupted config. What happened?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up once you claim to understand argument passing; usually phrased as a debugging story rather than a question.

The helper mutated the shared object instead of rebinding. The argument is a reference to the caller's dict, so cfg["timeout"] = 5 inside the helper writes straight through — there is no defensive copy anywhere in the path. If that dict is a module-level singleton, the mutation is permanent for the lifetime of the process, and every subsequent request sees it.

What makes this expensive to diagnose is that it is order-dependent and therefore intermittent. The first request through the helper behaves correctly; the damage only shows up in a later request that never touched the helper at all, so the stack trace points somewhere innocent. Under async or threaded serving it gets worse, because the interleaving decides who observes the half-mutated state.

The fix is to make copying explicit at the boundary — cfg = dict(caller_cfg) for a shallow copy, copy.deepcopy when nested structures are also mutated — or to remove the hazard by making the shared object immutable. This is the same bug as the mutable-default-argument trap: both come from assuming assignment copies when it shares.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

You're designing a request-scoped context object passed through a chain of async handlers. Mutation-through-alias has already caused one production incident. How do you design its binding semantics to prevent a repeat?

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat identity and mutation as an architectural property rather than a syntax detail.

The binding constraint is that a shared mutable object threaded through N handlers is a hidden global. Any handler can mutate state a later handler depends on, and Python's sharing semantics make that mutation invisible at the call site — nothing in handler(ctx) tells a reviewer whether ctx comes back changed. Under asyncio it is worse than under threads, because an await inside a handler hands control to a task that may be holding the same context, so the corruption is interleaving-dependent and will not reproduce under test.

So I would make the context immutable by construction: a frozen=True dataclass whose collection fields are tuples or frozensets rather than lists, since a frozen dataclass still happily hands out a mutable list attribute that anyone can append to. "Updating" then means ctx = replace(ctx, user=u), which returns a new object and rebinds one local name — the handler chain becomes a pipeline where each stage takes a context and returns a possibly-new one, and sharing is impossible rather than merely discouraged. Where genuinely per-task mutable scratch space is needed, that goes in a contextvars.ContextVar, which gives each task its own binding instead of one object shared across the loop.

The failure mode I'd instrument first is silent reuse of a module-level default — the case where every request gets the same context object because someone wrote it as a default argument or a module constant. A dev-mode middleware that records id(ctx) per request and asserts it has not been seen before catches that in the first minute of local testing, rather than at 3am when two requests interleave.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Operation Effect on the name Effect on the object Visible to aliases?
b = a binds b to a's object none — (now aliased)
b = a + [1] rebinds b to a new object none ❌ no
b.append(1) none mutates in place ✅ yes
b += [1] (list) rebinds to __iadd__'s result — the same object mutates in place ✅ yes
b += 1 (int) rebinds to a new int none (int is immutable) ❌ no
del b unbinds the name refcount −1; freed only at zero ❌ no
b[0] = 9 none mutates in place ✅ yes

11. What Goes Wrong

Two different failure modes sit under this heading: wrong beliefs about how binding works, which produce bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Python passes by value."

✅ Reality: Python passes object references by value. The reference is copied; the object is shared. Mutating the object affects the caller; rebinding the parameter does not.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "b = a makes an independent copy I can safely mutate."

✅ Reality: b = a makes an alias — id(a) == id(b), and b.append(x) is visible through a. Only an explicit copy(), deepcopy() or constructor call produces an independent object.

❌ Misconception: "x += y is just shorthand for x = x + y."

✅ Reality: For a list it calls __iadd__, mutates in place and every alias sees it; x = x + y would have built a new list and left aliases alone. For an int the two really are equivalent. Section 6 shows both in one paste.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

Binding is routinely conflated with copying and with mutation, and it is neither. Assignment binds a name and never copies — copying is copy.copy / copy.deepcopy, always an explicit call. Mutation changes the object and is visible through every name bound to it; rebinding changes which object a single name reaches and is visible through none. The two are independent axes, and a line of code does exactly one of them.

Interview Traps

  • Saying "Python is pass-by-reference" flatly — it invites the follow-up "then why doesn't reassigning the parameter change the caller's variable?", and there is no recovery. Say pass-by-object-reference and lead straight into the rebind-versus-mutate split.

  • Describing a = b as "copies b into a" — the word copy is the trap. It implies an independence that does not exist, and an interviewer who hears it will immediately hand you an aliasing puzzle.

  • Claiming += is always in-place — it is in-place for a list and a rebind for an int, and the difference is the type's __iadd__, not the syntax. Overstating either direction is the same mistake.

  • Explaining it entirely with id() and never naming a namespace — id(a) == id(b) is the evidence, not the mechanism. Saying STORE_FAST writes a pointer into a frame slot moves the answer up a level.

  • Not connecting it to a real bug — this topic is only interesting because of the shared-config and mutable-default incidents it explains. An answer that stays theoretical reads as memorised.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When TO use this

  • Deciding whether a function needs a defensive copy — if the function mutates an argument and the caller must not see it, the binding model tells you the mutation will propagate unless you copy at the boundary. This is the single most common application.

  • Designing "update returns a new value" APIs — frozen dataclasses, NamedTuple, functional pipelines. Each transform returns a new object and rebinds a local name, so aliasing surprises are structurally impossible.

  • Reasoning about lifetime and memory — binding increments a refcount, so knowing the rule tells you why an object survives del, why a long-lived list of references keeps a whole graph alive, and when memory is actually released.

  • Reading unfamiliar code fast — scanning for x.method() versus x = ... on a shared object is the quickest way to spot where state escapes.

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't rely on rebinding to "reset" a shared object — param = [] inside a function does not clear the caller's list, it only drops a local name. Use param.clear() when in-place reset is genuinely the intent, and say so in the signature.

  • Don't reach for deepcopy as the default defence — it is O(size), it will happily duplicate an entire object graph you meant to share, and it breaks on objects holding sockets, locks or file handles. Prefer a shallow copy at a narrow boundary, or immutability.

  • Don't pass shared mutable state across concurrency boundaries and manage it by discipline — aliasing plus async interleaving turns a shared object into an invisible global, and code review does not catch it. Use immutable context objects or contextvars.

  • Don't let the mental model stop at id() — identity of small ints and short strings is confounded by interning, so id() comparisons are a reliable teaching tool and an unreliable production check. Identity semantics belong to is, covered in the next note.

🔖 Version discipline

Binding semantics are stable across all of Python 3.x and are specified in the language reference, not left to the implementation — so nothing here is CPython-specific except the refcount detail and the exact bytecode names. Opcode names and the specialising interpreter's fast paths have changed across 3.11–3.13, so disassemble on your own interpreter rather than quoting LOAD_FAST as universal. The nearby moving part is small-object caching and interning, which affects the identity of the objects being bound rather than the binding rule itself.

13. Production Reality

This is the primitive underneath an entire family of production incidents, which is why it earns a CORE note despite being a one-sentence rule.

Why It Matters in Production

Every accidental shared-mutable bug — corrupted request config, a cache that changes shape on its own, a class default that accumulates across instances, a context object that leaks one user's state into another user's response — traces back to a team believing assignment copies. The line that causes it always looks innocent (self.defaults = incoming), passes review, and fails intermittently in a way that depends on request ordering, so it survives staging and shows up under production concurrency.

The business cost is a data-integrity incident rather than an outage: wrong data served correctly, which is worse, because monitoring does not catch it and the blast radius is however long it took someone to notice. Getting binding right is what turns "where do I need to copy?" into a deliberate, reviewable decision at a named boundary instead of a latent page.

Real World Usage

Not applicable — this is a language-level primitive without distinguishing production users. Its footprint is universal (every framework's request and context objects depend on it), but no system uses "names and binding" as a named feature.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Skipped — no defensible, citable benchmarks exist for a semantic rule, and per the no-fabrication rule no numbers beat invented numbers. The one number that matters is a semantic fact rather than a measurement: binding copies exactly one pointer, regardless of object size.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Binding is O(1) — one pointer write — no matter how large the object. The real cost hides in the defensive copies you must add to avoid aliasing bugs.
💰 Memory Sharing saves memory by never duplicating; defensive copies trade memory for isolation. deepcopy at a hot boundary is the version of this that shows up in an RSS graph.
🧮 CPU Negligible per bind; the refcount increment is a single add, serialized by the GIL on standard builds.
📈 Scale Shared mutable objects across requests or tasks become correctness bottlenecks long before they become performance bottlenecks.
🔧 Maintainability Explicit copy-at-boundary makes data flow reviewable. Implicit sharing hides it, and no type annotation expresses "I will mutate this".
🐍 CPython-specific Binding increments a refcount, tying names directly to the object-lifetime model; on free-threaded builds those increments contend across threads.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • CPython object model — names bind to heap PyObjects carrying a type pointer and a refcount.

  • Namespaces and LEGB scope — which slot a name resolves to, before binding decides what goes in it.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • is vs == and interning — identity of the objects that names get bound to.

  • Mutable vs immutable and the shared-default trap — the canonical binding-plus-mutation bug.

  • Copy semantics — the explicit escape hatch, and why shallow is usually the right depth.

  • Reference counting and GC — binding increments refcounts; rebinding and del decrement them.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Immutable data (frozen dataclass, NamedTuple, tuples over lists) — sidesteps aliasing by making "update" return a new object.

  • contextvars — per-task binding when one object shared across an event loop is unsafe.

🧩 Composes with

  • Function defaults — defaults are bound once at definition time, which is binding plus mutation producing the classic trap.

  • Decorators — @d is literally f = d(f), a rebinding of the function name.

  • copy.deepcopy — the explicit opt-out when sharing is not what you meant.

15. Lock it in

Assignment binds a name to an object — it never copies.
Mutation changes the object (all names see it); rebinding moves one name (no name sees it).

⚠️ The symmetry above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Optional: a story hook

🪝 Names are luggage tags, not suitcases.

You tie a second tag reading "b" onto a suitcase already tagged "a" — that is b = a: one bag, two tags, and no porter carried anything. Open the bag and add socks, and anyone reading either tag finds the socks there. Untie tag "b" and tie it to a different suitcase, and the first bag sits exactly where it was, still fully tagged "a".

Two tags on one suitcase is two names bound to one object, with id() equal. Adding socks is in-place mutation, visible through every name. Moving a tag is rebinding, which repoints exactly one name and leaves the object untouched.

What's the difference between is and ==, and which should you use for None?
Why does 256 is 256 return True but 257 is 257 sometimes return False?
A test suite passes locally but fails in CI with an assertion like assert record_id is expected_id on integer IDs. What's going on?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • is / identity — Comparisons: identity comparisons (is)

  • id() — Built-in functions: id

  • sys.intern — sys.intern

  • Bonus — Real Python: Python is vs ==: comparing objects

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — GeeksforGeeks: Difference between == and is operator in Python

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

This one is dangerous in a way most Python confusions aren't, because the wrong mental model keeps working for a while. You write if x is None and it's correct. You try if count is 5 and that works too. You compare two short strings with is and it comes back True. So you conclude the two operators are more or less interchangeable, and is is maybe the faster one.

Then the same code meets real data — a number above 256, a string that arrived over a socket — and it silently returns the wrong answer. Nothing crashes. The test suite still passes, because your test used small values.

The problem it solves is knowing which question you are actually asking, because Python gives you two operators for two genuinely different questions and the difference only surfaces under load. What to picture while reading: any object has two separate facts about it — what it is worth, and which object it is — and each operator reads a different one.

2. What Python normally does

Make two lists that look identical and ask both questions.

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]

They hold the same things, so comparing values says yes:

>>> a == b
True

But these are two lists. You built them separately, with two separate literals, and Python allocated two separate objects. The is operator asks that second question instead — are these the same object? — and gives the honest answer:

>>> a is b
False

You can see why, because every object carries an identity you can look at directly. id() hands it to you:

>>> id(a), id(b)
(4382916608, 4382913728)

Two different numbers, so two different objects. Conceptually that's all is does: fetch both identities and compare them.

a ──→ ┌─────────┐        b ──→ ┌─────────┐
      │ [1, 2]  │              │ [1, 2]  │
      │ id: …608│              │ id: …728│
      └─────────┘              └─────────┘

      a == b  →  compares the contents  →  True
      a is b  →  compares the ids       →  False

So the normal case is that equal and identical are different things, and Python answers them with different operators. Nothing surprising yet — which is exactly the problem, because it's about to look surprising.

3. What changes

Now run the same shape of code on small integers instead of lists.

x = 256
y = 256

Value equality behaves exactly as before:

>>> x == y
True

But identity flips:

>>> x is y
True

Same two-assignment pattern, opposite answer. And it isn't stable either — push the number up by one:

>>> p = 257
>>> q = 257
>>> p is q          # at the REPL, two separate compilations
False

So 256 is 256 is True and 257 is 257 is False, on the same interpreter, seconds apart. That is the moment most people conclude is is unreliable or magical.

So is is doing something different for ints?

No — and this is the important bit. is did precisely what it did before: it compared two identities and reported whether they matched. The behaviour that changed is which objects you were handed.

In CPython, the integers from −5 to 256 are created once, at interpreter startup, and reused forever. When you write 256 twice you don't get two objects — you get the same cached one, twice. So is returns True because they genuinely are the same object, not because it decided to compare values this time.

Above that range there's no cache, so 257 generally builds a fresh object each time and identity is False. (Generally, not always — see Section 6, where a second mechanism muddies it further.)

Strings have their own version of this. Identifier-like literals get interned at compile time, so two occurrences share one object, while a string built at runtime does not:

>>> s1 = "admin"
>>> s2 = "".join(["ad", "min"])
>>> s1 == s2
True
>>> s1 is s2
False

And in case the picture is still "is is basically == but stricter", here is the pair going the other way:

>>> n = float("nan")
>>> n == n
False
>>> n is n
True

One object compared with itself. Identity says yes, because it obviously is the same object. Equality says no, because IEEE-754 says NaN equals nothing, including itself.

The trade, stated plainly: is never lies about identity, but identity is almost never the question you meant to ask — and CPython's caches make the wrong question return the right answer often enough to hide the bug.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

The two operators compile to different bytecode and take completely different paths.

is compiles to IS_OP: a raw pointer comparison between the two PyObject * operands. No method call, no dispatch, no user code — which is why it can never be overridden and never raises. == compiles to COMPARE_OP, which enters the rich-comparison protocol and calls __eq__, with reflection to the right-hand operand if the left one returns NotImplemented.

That difference is the whole reason == can be made to lie:

>>> class Sneaky:
...     def __eq__(self, other): return True
>>> Sneaky() == None
True
>>> Sneaky() is None
False

The caches that cause the surprises sit underneath object creation, not inside either operator:

There is a second mechanism layered on top of the small-int cache, and it explains why 257 is 257 is not even consistently False. Within a single compilation unit — one function body, one module, one exec — the compiler folds equal constants into one entry in the code object's constant table. So p = 257; q = 257 inside one function gives True, while the same two lines typed separately at the REPL give False, because each REPL line is compiled on its own. I verified both, and Section 6 lets you reproduce it.

That is the real lesson of the mechanism: the answer depends on how your source was compiled, which is not a property of your program's logic at all. Python itself flags this — since 3.8, writing is against a literal raises a SyntaxWarning: "is" with a literal. Did you mean "=="? at compile time.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4

def is_admin_broken(role: str) -> bool:
    # ❌ identity check on a value that may not be interned.
    #    Passes every unit test written with the literal "admin".
    return role is "admin"          # SyntaxWarning since 3.8 — listen to it

def is_admin(role: str) -> bool:
    # ✅ value comparison: correct regardless of where the string came from
    return role == "admin"

# In a test:            role = "admin"              -> interned literal
# From a request body:  role = json.loads(...)      -> fresh object
parsed = "".join(["ad", "min"])     # stands in for a runtime-built string

print(is_admin_broken(parsed))      # False  <- silently denies a real admin
print(is_admin(parsed))             # True

# The one place identity IS the semantics: singletons and sentinels.
MISSING = object()                  # unique, unforgeable sentinel

def get(cfg: dict, key: str, default=MISSING):
    value = cfg.get(key, MISSING)
    if value is MISSING:            # ✅ identity is exactly the question
        if default is MISSING:
            raise KeyError(key)
        return default
    return value

6. Break it yourself

Two experiments. The first shows the cache boundary; the second shows that compilation, not logic, decides the answer.

import sys

def same_unit():                 # both literals in ONE code object
    p = 257
    q = 257
    return p is q

g = {}
exec("m = 257", g)               # two SEPARATE compilations
exec("n = 257", g)

print(256 is 256, 257 is 257)    # cache boundary
print(same_unit())               # ?
print(g["m"] is g["n"])          # ?

# what to look for: same value 257, two different answers
# naive model would predict: 257 is 257 gives one consistent answer either way

You get True from same_unit() and False across the two exec calls — I verified both on 3.9.6. The value is identical in every case; what differs is whether the compiler had the chance to fold the two constants into one.

A shorter one for strings, which is the version that actually bites in production:

s1 = "admin"
s2 = "".join(["ad", "min"])
print(s1 == s2, s1 is s2)              # True False
print(sys.intern(s2) is s1)            # True — interning forces sharing

# what to look for: two strings that are equal but not identical
# naive model would predict: equal strings are the same string

What both prove is that identity is a fact about object lifetime and allocation, not about your data — so any check built on it is really a check on CPython's memory behaviour.

7. The deeper mental model

Back up, and the split you've been looking at turns out to run through the whole language:

           one object                two objects, equal values

           x ──→ ┌───────┐          a ──→ ┌───────┐   b ──→ ┌───────┐
                 │ value │                │ value │         │ value │
                 └───────┘                └───────┘         └───────┘

  identity:      x is x  → True           a is b  → False
  value:         x == x  → True*          a == b  → True
                        (*unless NaN)

Once you see identity and value as two independent axes, a whole family of Python questions collapses into one distinction:

  • is vs == — the operators for each axis.
  • copy() vs deepcopy() — whether you duplicate the identity or the values underneath it.
  • Mutable default arguments — one object reused across calls, which is an identity fact that surprises you as a value bug.
  • __eq__ and __hash__ — the contract that says objects equal by value must agree on hash, so dicts can treat them interchangeably despite different identities.
  • weakref and WeakSet — tracking objects by identity, with lifetime made explicit.

So the useful reframing isn't "remember to use ==". It is that Python lets you ask about an object's identity as a first-class question, and the moment you reach for is, you should be able to say why identity — rather than value — is what you actually meant. There are only a few honest answers: it's a singleton (None, True, False), it's a sentinel you created to be unforgeable, or you're genuinely tracking object lifetime.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
is compares what? == compares what? is → identity (same object, equal id()); == → value, via __eq__.
Which bytecode does each emit? is → IS_OP (pointer compare, no dispatch); == → COMPARE_OP → __eq__.
Small-int cache range? −5 to 256, allocated once at startup; is is True on those by accident.
Why is 257 is 257 inconsistent? Within one compilation unit the compiler folds the constants (True); across units, distinct objects (False).
When is is correct? Singletons — None, True, False — and sentinel objects you made yourself.
One case where == is False but is is True? n = float("nan"): n == n is False, n is n is True.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you actually get before the interviewer follows up.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What's the difference between is and ==, and which should you use for None?

== asks whether two objects have the same value, by calling __eq__. is asks whether they're the same object, by comparing identity — a raw pointer check that runs no user code. Use == for values. For None use is, because there's exactly one None per interpreter, and __eq__ can be overridden to lie.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Why does 256 is 256 return True but 257 is 257 sometimes return False?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know this is an allocation artefact rather than operator behaviour.

CPython pre-allocates the integers from −5 to 256 once at startup and hands back the same object every time one of those values is produced. So is returns True for them because they genuinely are one object — the operator did nothing special. It's a memory optimisation, not a language guarantee, and other implementations need not do it.

Above the cache there's no shared object, but the answer still isn't stable, because a second mechanism applies: within a single compilation unit the compiler folds equal constants into one entry in the code object. So p = 257; q = 257 inside one function is True, while the same two statements typed as separate REPL lines are False — I verified both on 3.9.6. The honest answer is "it depends on how the source was compiled," which is exactly why identity checks against non-singletons are never correct. Python agrees: since 3.8 is against a literal emits a SyntaxWarning.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A test suite passes locally but fails in CI with an assertion like assert record_id is expected_id on integer IDs. What's going on?

📍 Seen in the wild: the classic small-int-cache bug.

Someone used is where they meant ==, on values that land inside the small-int cache locally and outside it in CI's data. With IDs up to 256 both sides hit the same cached object and the identity check passes by luck; the first time an ID is 257 or larger the two equal integers are distinct objects and is returns False. The bug was always present — the cache was masking it.

The string version is worse because it's security-relevant. if role is "admin" passes every unit test, where the literal is interned and shared, then fails in production once role arrives from JSON or a socket as a freshly allocated object. The check silently denies a genuine admin, or — with the comparison inverted — grants access it shouldn't. Both fix the same way: use ==, because identity was never the intended semantics.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

You're building a high-throughput dedup layer that must decide "have I already seen this?" across millions of events. When is identity the right tool, and where does it break at scale?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know identity is about object lifetime, not value, and won't misuse id() as a hash.

Identity is right only when you genuinely mean this same object instance — a visited-set in a graph traversal to break cycles, or a WeakSet of objects already processed while they're still alive. There is and id() are O(1) and exactly correct.

The constraint that decides everything is object lifetime. id() is only unique among live objects: once an object is garbage-collected, CPython is free to reuse its address, so a long-lived set of raw id() integers will eventually alias a freed object to a new one and report a false "seen". That's a correctness bug whose rate rises with GC pressure, which makes it maddening to reproduce.

For value-based dedup across millions of events I wouldn't use identity at all — two events that are equal but distinct objects must dedup together, and is cannot see that. I'd hash a normalised payload into a set, or a Bloom filter or Redis if the cardinality doesn't fit in memory. If I did need identity tracking of live objects, I'd hold weak references so entries drop as objects die, and never persist bare id() values across a GC boundary.

The signal I'd monitor first is a false-dedup rate correlated with GC activity — that correlation is the signature of id() reuse.

10. Quick Comparison Table

is ==
Asks are these the same object? do these have the same value?
Bytecode IS_OP — pointer compare COMPARE_OP → __eq__
Runs user code? never yes, and it may raise
Overridable? no yes, via __eq__
Correct for None, True, False, sentinels, lifetime tracking everything else
Fails you when caching/interning makes it accidentally True __eq__ is written to lie
NaN n is n → True n == n → False

11. What Goes Wrong

Two failure modes: wrong beliefs about what the operators do, which ship bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "is is just a faster ==."

✅ Reality: They answer different questions. is is faster because it does less — a pointer compare instead of a method call — but it's answering same object?, not same value?. Choosing it for speed is choosing the wrong question quickly.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "is on two equal strings is fine, strings are immutable."

✅ Reality: Immutability has nothing to do with it. Interning does, and only compile-time, identifier-like literals get interned automatically. A string built at runtime is a distinct object with the same value.

❌ Misconception: "If a == b is True, then a is b might as well be."

✅ Reality: Nearly backwards. a is b implies a == b for well-behaved types, never the reverse — and even that implication breaks on NaN, where n is n is True while n == n is False.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

is is routinely conflated with ==, and separately with hash(). All three are different axes: identity is which object, equality is what value, and hashing is a value-derived bucket that must agree with __eq__. Two objects can be equal and hash-equal while having entirely different identities — that's the normal case, and it's what makes dicts work.

Interview Traps

  • Saying "is compares memory addresses" without adding that this is CPython-specific. id() is defined as a unique constant integer for the object's lifetime; that it happens to be an address is an implementation detail.

  • Explaining the small-int cache but not constant folding — you'll get 257 is 257 returning True in a follow-up and have no explanation for it.

  • Recommending is for performance. Signals that you think they're interchangeable.

  • Forgetting the __eq__-can-lie argument for is None. "It's the convention" is a junior answer; "a class can override __eq__ to return True against None" is the real one.

  • Not mentioning the SyntaxWarning. Since 3.8 Python tells you about this at compile time, and knowing that shows you've actually hit it.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When is is correct

  • Singletons — x is None, flag is True, flag is False. There is exactly one of each per interpreter, so identity is the semantics.

  • Sentinel objects — a module-level MISSING = object() to distinguish "argument not passed" from "passed as None". Unforgeable by construction, which is the point.

  • Lifetime and cycle tracking — visited-sets in graph traversal, WeakSet of already-processed objects, or any question genuinely about this instance.

  • Enum members — colour is Colour.RED is idiomatic, since enum members are singletons by design.

⚠️ When NOT to use is

  • On any value that came from outside your process — parsed JSON, socket data, a database row. Interning and caching don't apply, so identity is effectively random.

  • On numbers, unless you can prove the value stays inside −5..256 and the compilation unit can't change. You can't, so don't.

  • As an optimisation for ==. If the profiler says __eq__ is hot, fix __eq__.

  • Across a GC boundary via stored id() values — addresses are reused once objects die, which turns a stale id() into a false match.

🔖 Version discipline

The −5..256 cache range, constant folding behaviour, and which strings get interned are all CPython implementation details, not language guarantees — PyPy, MicroPython and others may differ, and CPython has changed interning behaviour between releases. (Verified 19 Sep 2026 on CPython 3.9.6: 256 is 256 → True; 257 is 257 → True inside one code object, False across two exec units; "".join(["ad","min"]) is "admin" → False.) The SyntaxWarning for is against a literal arrived in 3.8.

13. Production Reality

This is the rare language-fundamentals topic that shows up in incident reports, because the failure is silent, data-dependent, and passes review by reading naturally.

Why It Matters in Production

A check like if role is "admin" is correct in every test that uses the literal and wrong the moment the value arrives over the wire, which means it ships. There's no exception and no log line — the branch simply doesn't take, and a real admin gets a permission error, or an authorisation check quietly evaluates the wrong way. The same shape appears on integer IDs, where it survives until a record crosses 256. Both are latent bugs whose trigger is data volume or data source, so they reach production by construction: the conditions that expose them don't exist in a test fixture.

The defence is cheap and worth stating as a rule: is is only correct against None, True, False, an enum member, or a sentinel you created. Anywhere else, it's a bug waiting for bigger inputs. Modern linters enforce exactly this — Ruff's F632 and Pylint's literal-comparison flag identity checks against literals, and since 3.8 the interpreter itself emits a SyntaxWarning.

Real World Usage

The sentinel pattern is the everyday legitimate use: MISSING = object() (or _sentinel) at module level, then if value is MISSING, which is how dataclasses, attrs and much of the standard library distinguish "not supplied" from "supplied as None". sys.intern shows up in high-volume parsers that compare or dict-key the same strings repeatedly — interning up front makes hashing cheaper and shrinks memory, which is the one place you deliberately manufacture shared identity. And WeakSet/weakref is the standard tool when you need identity tracking without pinning objects alive.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Metric Value Context Source
Small-int cache range −5 to 256 shared objects, allocated at startup CPython implementation detail; verified 3.9.6
SyntaxWarning for literal is Python 3.8+ compile-time, not runtime CPython changelog; verified 3.9.6

⚠️ These are CPython behaviours, not language guarantees. Re-verify on your target interpreter and don't quote the cache range as portable.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency is is a pointer compare with no dispatch, so it is genuinely faster — but only correct for the handful of cases below. Speed is never the reason to choose it.
🔒 Correctness is cannot be overridden or made to raise, which is exactly why it's the right check for None when __eq__ may be hostile.
🧮 Memory Interning and the small-int cache exist to save memory by sharing objects; the identity confusion is a side effect, not the purpose.
🔧 Maintainability An is on a non-singleton is a time bomb keyed to input size or source. Linters catch the literal form; they cannot catch a is b on two variables.
🐍 CPython-specific Cache range, constant folding and auto-interning are all implementation details. Code that depends on them is not portable Python.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • Names and binding — a name is a label bound to an object, which is what makes "same object" a meaningful question at all.

  • CPython object model — every object has an identity, a type and a refcount.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • __eq__ / __hash__ contract — the rules that let value-equal objects with different identities behave interchangeably in dicts and sets.

  • Copy semantics — copy vs deepcopy is the same identity/value split applied to duplication.

  • weakref and object lifetime — identity tracking without keeping objects alive.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • == — the default for anything that isn't a singleton. This is almost always the answer.

  • math.isnan() — for the NaN case specifically, since neither operator does what you want.

  • Content hashing — when you mean "same value" across process or machine boundaries, where identity has no meaning at all.

🧩 Composes with

  • Sentinel objects — MISSING = object() is designed to be compared with is.

  • enum.Enum — members are singletons, so is is the idiomatic comparison.

  • sys.intern — deliberately manufacturing shared identity for hashing and memory wins.

15. Lock it in

`==` asks "same value?" and calls your code.
`is`  asks "same object?" and cannot be fooled — or reasoned with.

⚠️ The symmetry line above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Story hook (optional)

is = same passport; == = same face.

Two people can have identical faces — value-equal — while carrying different passports, like twins. None is the one celebrity there's only ever a single copy of, so checking the passport (x is None) is how you know it's really them. CPython keeps a photo album of the famous small numbers −5 to 256 and the interned words, and everyone in that album shares one passport — which is what fools is into insisting two separate-looking things are the same person.

Passport = id() · face = __eq__ · the photo album = the small-int cache and string interning.

notes.title: Mutable vs Immutable & the Shared-Default Trap
