notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Default parameter values — Function definitions: default parameter values

  • Hashable — Glossary: hashable

  • The dataclasses fix — dataclasses.field(default_factory=…)

  • Bonus — Ruff: B006 mutable-argument-default

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: Python's mutable vs immutable types

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

This one is unusual because it is not conceptually hard — it is one sentence long — and yet it keeps shipping. The reason is that the broken code reads perfectly naturally, passes review, passes tests, and only misbehaves after a function has been called several times in the same process, which is exactly the thing a unit test does not do.

The problem it solves is a whole family of "why is this function remembering things?" bugs: a helper whose returned list keeps growing, a cache nobody declared, one tenant's data appearing in another tenant's response. All of them are the same bug wearing different clothes.

So hold this question the whole way through: when does the expression after = in a function signature actually run? Get that one right and the entire trap, along with its fix, follows without memorising anything.

2. What Python normally does

Here is a signature with a default, of the kind you write without a second thought.

def greet(name, greeting="hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}"

Nothing surprising happens when you call it, so the interesting question is not what it returns but where that string "hello" is being kept between calls. It has to live somewhere — and it does, on the function object itself:

>>> greet.__defaults__
('hello',)

That is a real tuple, attached to a real object, sitting in memory for as long as the function exists. Which means the default was built at some point before you called anything. When?

The cleanest way to see it is to use a default that changes every time it is evaluated, and then not call the function for a while:

>>> import time
>>> def stamp(t=time.time()):
...     return t
...
>>> stamp(); time.sleep(2); stamp()
1758326400.12
1758326400.12

Two seconds apart, identical answer. time.time() did not run on either call — it ran once, when the def statement itself executed, and the result has been sitting in stamp.__defaults__ ever since.

That is the fact underneath everything else here. def is not a declaration the compiler notes down; it is a statement that executes, and executing it evaluates every default expression, packs the results into a tuple, and hangs that tuple off the new function object:

function object "greet"
 ├── __code__      (the compiled body)
 └── __defaults__ ──→ ("hello",)        built once, at def-time
                          ▲
                          └── every call that omits `greeting`
                              binds the parameter to THIS object

So a default value is one object, created once when the def runs, and shared by every call that omits the argument.

3. What changes

Nothing about that rule changes. What changes is the type you put in the slot — and that turns a harmless piece of sharing into a leak.

def collect(x, acc=[]):
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

Same shape as greet, same rule applying to it. But now watch three ordinary calls:

>>> collect(1)
[1]
>>> collect(2)
[1, 2]
>>> collect(3)
[1, 2, 3]

The second call already sees what the first left behind. Nothing here is a special case — it is exactly the Section 2 rule, plus one extra fact: a list can be changed in place, and "hello" cannot.

That is the entire difference, and it is worth being precise about it. The immutable default is shared too. Every call to greet binds greeting to the very same string object. It simply does not matter, because there is no operation that could alter it — the worst any call can do is rebind its own local name and leave the stored object untouched.

IMMUTABLE DEFAULT               MUTABLE DEFAULT

__defaults__ ──→ "hello"        __defaults__ ──→ [1, 2, 3]
                   ▲                                ▲
call 1 ──┐         │            call 1 ──┐          │
call 2 ──┼─────────┘            call 2 ──┼──────────┘
call 3 ──┘                      call 3 ──┘

shared, and harmless:           shared, and every call's
nothing can change it           append is permanent

And the fix falls straight out of the picture, because it does not fight the rule — it puts something unmutatable in the slot and builds the real object inside the body, where code runs per call:

def collect(x, acc=None):
    acc = [] if acc is None else acc      # runs on every call
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

>>> collect(1)
[1]
>>> collect(2)
[2]

The trade in one sentence: Python evaluates defaults once so that calls stay cheap, and you pay for that by owning the decision of whether the stored default is something a caller could change.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Conceptually, defaults are baked in when the function is created. In CPython the sequence is visible in the bytecode of the enclosing scope, which is the detail that makes the timing undeniable.

When the module runs, the default expressions are evaluated as ordinary code in the enclosing scope, pushed onto the stack, and handed to MAKE_FUNCTION, which attaches them to the new function object as __defaults__. The function body is not involved at all — it has not run yet, and will not until someone calls it.

Follow the stages and notice what the call-time step does not do. Argument binding copies a pointer out of __defaults__ into the parameter's local slot. It does not re-run the expression, it does not copy the object, and it has no way of knowing whether the object it is handing over is pristine or has been scribbled on by forty previous calls. That is the same pointer-store you have already seen in plain assignment, which is why this topic is really binding-plus-mutation with a longer fuse.

Two consequences are worth naming because they are what interviewers push on. The first is that the shared default is function-level state with process lifetime — it is not reset between calls, between requests, or between test cases in the same run, only when the module is re-imported into a fresh interpreter. The second is that dataclasses refuse to let you do this at all: a mutable default on a field raises ValueError when the class body executes, which is the language enforcing the fix rather than documenting it.

Underneath both sits the mutable/immutable split itself, and it is a property of the type, not of how you use it. An immutable type offers no operation that alters the object, so every "change" allocates a new one and rebinds. That is also why immutability and hashability travel together: hash() must return the same value for an object's whole life for dict and set lookup to work, and a type that cannot change can promise that trivially.

5. Code / Config Example

The production shape is all three forms side by side — the bug, the standard fix, and the case where the standard fix is itself subtly wrong.

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

_MISSING = object()                       # private sentinel: distinct from None

def add_tag(item, tags=[]):               # ❌ one list, built at def-time,
    tags.append(item)                     #    shared by every default-using call
    return tags

def add_tag_ok(item, tags=None):          # ✅ the idiom: immutable sentinel,
    tags = [] if tags is None else tags   #    real object built per call
    tags.append(item)
    return tags

def retry(fn, backoff=_MISSING):          # ✅ when None is a MEANINGFUL value —
    if backoff is _MISSING:               #    here None means "no backoff at all",
        backoff = [1, 2, 4]               #    so it can't double as "omitted"
    return backoff

@dataclass
class Job:
    name: str
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # the language enforces this:
                                                    # `tags: list = []` raises
                                                    # ValueError at class creation

Three tools, three different situations. add_tag_ok is what you write almost always. The _MISSING sentinel is for the case the None idiom cannot express — a parameter where None is a legitimate argument a caller might pass on purpose, so you need a third state meaning "nothing was supplied". And field(default_factory=list) is the same fix with the decision taken away from you, which is why dataclass fields never exhibit this bug.

6. Break it yourself

Paste this in. It prints the identity of the stored default across calls, which turns "the default is shared" from a claim into an address you can read.

def collect(x, acc=[]):
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

print(id(collect.__defaults__[0]), collect(1))
print(id(collect.__defaults__[0]), collect(2))
print(id(collect.__defaults__[0]), collect(3))

def broken_fix(x, acc=None):
    acc = acc or []                 # the "clever" one-liner
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

mine = []
broken_fix(1, mine)
print(mine)                         # ?

# what to look for: one constant id across all three calls while the list grows,
#                   and then an explicitly-passed empty list that gets ignored
# naive model would predict: a different id each call, and mine == [1]

The id never changes — one object, growing [1] → [1, 2] → [1, 2, 3] — and mine prints [], not [1].

Both halves are worth sitting with. The first proves the default is a single long-lived object hanging off the function, not something rebuilt per call. The second is the reason the fix must be acc is None and never acc or []: an explicitly-passed empty list is falsy, so or throws away the caller's object and silently builds a different one. The caller's list never gets the append, and nothing raises. Same class of bug as the original, introduced by the fix for it.

7. The deeper mental model

Step back and this stops being a gotcha about lists and becomes a question about when code runs:

      DEF-TIME                          CALL-TIME
  (runs once, when the             (runs every time, when
   statement is executed)           the function is invoked)

  default expressions      ───┐     the function body
  decorator application       │     the None-sentinel line
  class bodies                │     comprehension bodies
  annotations (pre-PEP 649)   │
                              │
                              └──→ anything built here is
                                   ONE object, for the life
                                   of the process

Python has very few places where code runs once and a lot of places where it runs repeatedly, and almost every "why is this remembering things?" bug is something that landed in the left column when the author meant the right one. The mutable default is the famous one. Its siblings are the same shape: a decorator that accumulates state because the decorator body ran once at import; a class attribute that behaves like a global because the class body ran once; a closure over a loop variable that reads the last value because the lookup was deferred to call-time when you wanted def-time.

Immutability is what makes the left column safe. If the object in the shared slot cannot be altered, it does not matter how many callers reach it, and that is a bargain the language offers everywhere — tuples over lists at boundaries, frozen=True on dataclasses, frozenset as a dict key.

So the honest one-line summary is not "don't use mutable defaults". It is that sharing is fine; sharing something mutable is what costs you — and the fix is always to move the construction into the column where code runs per call.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
When is a default argument evaluated? Once, at function-definition time — when the def statement executes.
Where does the default object live? In a tuple on the function object: f.__defaults__ (keyword-only: __kwdefaults__).
Why does def f(x, acc=[]) accumulate? Every default-using call binds to that one list; mutations persist on the function.
The fix? acc=None, then acc = [] if acc is None else acc — a fresh object per call.
Why not acc = acc or []? An explicitly-passed empty list is falsy and gets silently discarded.
What makes an object hashable? A __hash__ that is stable for the object's life — which effectively requires immutability of the hashed state.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Skipped — the concept here is a timing rule rather than a structure, and the def-time-versus-call-time table in Section 7 is already the memorable form of it.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you get before the follow-up lands. Everything below Tier 1 is what they follow up with.

Tier 1 — Verifier

Why is def f(x, acc=[]) a bug?

The default is evaluated once, when the def statement executes, and the resulting list is stored on the function object in f.__defaults__. It is not rebuilt per call.

So every call that omits the argument binds the parameter to that same list, and any .append() accumulates across calls — the second caller sees what the first left behind. The fix is acc=None plus acc = [] if acc is None else acc, which builds a fresh list inside the body, where code actually runs per call.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Where does the default value physically live, and why does that explain the trap?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can point at __defaults__ and the def-time/call-time split, or only recite the rule.

When the def statement executes, each default expression is evaluated as ordinary code in the enclosing scope and the results are handed to MAKE_FUNCTION, which stores them as a tuple on the function: f.__defaults__ for positional defaults, f.__kwdefaults__ for keyword-only ones. This happens exactly once, at import time for a module-level function.

At call time, a missing argument causes the interpreter to copy the corresponding pointer out of __defaults__ into the parameter's local slot. It does not re-evaluate the expression and it does not copy the object. So the mutable default is a single long-lived object hanging off the function — function-level shared state with process lifetime. You can watch it directly: id(f.__defaults__[0]) stays constant across calls while the list grows [1] → [1,2] → [1,2,3]. Immutable defaults never show the bug because there is no operation that alters them; the worst a call can do is rebind its own local name.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A caching helper, def fetch(key, _cache={}), works fine in tests but leaks memory and returns stale cross-tenant data in production. Diagnose it.

📍 Seen in the wild: the usual escalation once you have answered Tier 1 — the same mechanism, dressed as a plausible optimisation.

_cache={} is one dict created at def-time and shared by every call for the life of the process. As an accidental module-global cache it grows without bound, because nothing ever evicts from it — that is the memory leak, and it ends as an OOMKilled worker at whatever hour traffic peaks. And because it is shared across all callers rather than scoped to anything, a key that collides across tenants hands one tenant's cached value to another, which is a data-isolation breach rather than a performance bug.

Tests miss both halves for structural reasons. A short test run never grows the dict enough to leak, and single-tenant fixtures never exercise the cross-tenant path, so the helper looks correct right up until it is serving real traffic.

The fix depends on what was actually intended. If the author wanted per-call freshness, it is the None sentinel. If they genuinely wanted a cache, then the sharing is correct but everything around it is missing: make it an explicit, named, bounded component — functools.lru_cache(maxsize=N), or a module-level cache with eviction and a key that includes the tenant — so that the sharing and its bounds are visible to a reviewer instead of hidden in a parameter list.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

You're standardising function signatures across a large service where mutable-default bugs have shipped twice. Design the conventions and guardrails so this class of bug cannot reach production.

🎯 Really testing: whether you convert a language gotcha into an enforceable engineering control rather than a style-guide sentence.

The binding constraint is that this bug is invisible to both of the defences a team normally relies on. It is invisible in review, because the broken signature reads more naturally than the fixed one, and invisible in tests, because a single call never exhibits it. Two incidents have already demonstrated that developer vigilance is not the control. So the guardrail has to be mechanical.

Concretely, I would make the correct pattern the only one the toolchain permits: enable the mutable-default rule (Ruff B006, or flake8-bugbear's equivalent), fail CI on it rather than warning, and codify the None-sentinel idiom in the style guide with the acc or [] anti-fix called out explicitly, since that is the failure mode of a half-learned rule. For parameters where None is itself a meaningful value, standardise one shared _MISSING = object() sentinel so there is a single recognisable idiom rather than five local inventions.

Structurally, I would push the boundary types toward immutability — frozen dataclasses and tuples for anything crossing a service or module boundary — so that even an accidental shared default cannot be mutated; it raises instead of silently accumulating. And where shared state is genuinely wanted, it must be an explicit named component with a bound and an eviction policy, never a bare mutable default acting as one.

The failure mode I would instrument first is RSS growth in a long-lived worker that does not track request volume. That is the signature of an accidental process-lifetime cache quietly accumulating, and it is the cheapest alert to add for a bug class whose whole problem is that it does not announce itself.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Immutable (int, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes) Mutable (list, dict, set, most objects)
In-place change? impossible — operations return new objects yes — methods mutate the same object
Safe as a default arg? ✅ always (nothing can be changed) ❌ never, unless sharing is the intent
Hashable / usable as a dict key? ✅ yes ❌ no (__hash__ is None)
+= behaviour rebinds to a new object mutates in place via __iadd__
Aliasing risk none high — every name is a live window
In a dataclass field x: int = 0 is fine must use field(default_factory=list)

11. What Goes Wrong

Two different failure modes sit under this heading: wrong beliefs about how defaults work, which produce bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Default arguments are re-created fresh on every call."

✅ Reality: They are evaluated once when the def executes and stored in f.__defaults__. A mutable default is one shared object reused by every call that omits the argument.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "def f(x=[]) is fine as long as I don't reassign x inside the body."

✅ Reality: It is the exact opposite. Reassigning is harmless — it only repoints a local name. Mutating is the bug, because the shared object in __defaults__ is what accumulates.

❌ Misconception: "Tuples are immutable, so a tuple default is always safe."

✅ Reality: A tuple freezes references, not referents. def f(x=([],)) still shares one inner list, and x[0].append(1) accumulates across calls exactly as before.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

Mutable-versus-immutable gets conflated with hashable-versus-unhashable, and they are linked but not the same thing. Immutability of the hashed state is what makes a stable __hash__ possible, which is why most immutable built-ins are hashable and most mutable ones are not. But the correspondence is not exact in either direction: you can define a hashable class with mutable fields that are excluded from the hash, and a tuple containing a list is unhashable despite the tuple itself being immutable.

Interview Traps

  • Saying "the default is created on each call" — the exact inverse of the truth, and the single most common wrong answer. It ends the line of questioning badly.

  • Fixing it with acc = acc or [] — subtly broken, because an explicitly-passed empty list, 0 or "" is falsy and gets silently replaced. Say acc is None, and say why you are not using truthiness.

  • Never naming __defaults__ — pointing at where the object physically lives is what separates understanding the mechanism from having memorised the symptom.

  • Claiming tuples are "fully immutable" — they freeze references, not referents, and interviewers probe this exact edge as the follow-up.

  • Treating it as a trivia question — the reason it is asked is the production version (an unbounded shared cache, cross-tenant bleed). An answer that never reaches a real failure reads as recited.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When TO use this

  • Immutable defaults, freely — def f(x=0, name="", opts=()) is always safe, needs no sentinel, and avoids a per-call allocation entirely because there is nothing to build.

  • The None sentinel whenever a parameter's default should be a fresh mutable object per call. It is the standard, instantly recognisable, lint-enforceable idiom, and it should be the reflex.

  • A private _MISSING = object() sentinel when None is itself a valid argument a caller might pass deliberately, so "omitted" and "explicitly None" stay distinguishable.

  • A mutable default on purpose, as a documented memoisation cache, only when process-lifetime sharing is genuinely the goal — and even then, prefer naming it as an explicit structure so the intent is legible in review.

  • field(default_factory=…) for every dataclass field holding a collection. The language raises if you forget, so this is the one place the fix is free.

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Never use a mutable literal as a default when you want per-call freshness — list, dict, set and default-constructed objects all share across calls, and none of them announce it.

  • Don't use a mutable default as a cache without a bound — it grows for the process lifetime with no eviction, which is a memory leak with extra steps. Use lru_cache(maxsize=…) or a real cache with a TTL.

  • Don't use None as the sentinel if None is a legitimate argument value — you will be unable to tell "the caller passed None" from "the caller passed nothing", and the resulting bug is worse than the one you were fixing.

  • Don't rely on the None idiom inside a hot loop without thinking about the allocation — it costs one comparison and one object per call, which is noise in a request handler and measurable in a tight numeric loop. That is a reason to restructure, not a reason to use a mutable default.

🔖 Version discipline

Def-time evaluation of defaults is specified in the language reference and is stable across all of Python 3.x — this is not going to change, and dataclasses enforce the safe form outright. The linter rule identifier (Ruff B006) is current as of the Created date; confirm the exact code in your own toolchain, since rule numbering does move between major releases. One nearby thing genuinely is in flux: PEP 649 changed annotation evaluation timing in 3.14, which is a different slot in the same signature — it does not affect defaults, and conflating the two is a mistake worth avoiding out loud.

13. Production Reality

This is one of the highest-frequency real bugs in Python codebases, and its cost is out of all proportion to how simple the rule is.

Why It Matters in Production

An accidental shared default is process-lifetime state that nobody declared. In its mild form it is an unbounded cache that grows until a worker is OOMKilled at 3am, with no corresponding growth in traffic to explain it. In its serious form it is a data-isolation failure: one request's accumulated list appears in a later request's response, which is wrong data served with a 200, so monitoring stays green and the blast radius is however long it takes a human to notice.

What makes it expensive rather than merely common is that every defence a team has fails on it. The signature reads naturally, so review passes it. A single call behaves correctly, so unit tests pass it. It only surfaces under sustained multi-call load in a long-lived process, which is production. Understanding def-time evaluation is what lets you — and, more reliably, your linter — stop it at the door.

Real World Usage

Not applicable — this is a language-level gotcha rather than a distinguishing production feature. Its fix is pervasive: the None-sentinel idiom appears throughout the standard library and every major framework's signatures, and dataclasses.field(default_factory=…) is the same fix promoted into the language.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Skipped — this is a semantic timing rule, not a performance characteristic, and there are no defensible citable benchmarks. Per the no-fabrication rule, no numbers beat invented ones.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency The None-sentinel fix costs one identity comparison and one allocation per call — negligible outside a tight numeric loop.
💰 Memory The bug's cost is unbounded growth of a shared object for the process lifetime; the fix bounds it to per-call lifetime.
🧮 CPU Immutable defaults avoid per-call allocation entirely, since there is nothing to construct.
📈 Scale Accidental shared defaults are correctness and stability failures under sustained load, not throughput problems — they get worse the longer a worker lives.
🔧 Maintainability The None idiom is instantly recognisable and lint-enforceable; a mutable default is a silent landmine that reads better than the correct code.
🐍 CPython-specific Nothing here is implementation-specific — __defaults__ and def-time evaluation are specified, so the behaviour is identical on PyPy and other implementations.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • Names, binding and assignment — the default is a bound object, and call-time binding copies its pointer rather than the object.

  • Mutable versus immutable types — only a mutable default can exhibit the trap at all.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • dataclasses — field(default_factory=…) is this fix, enforced by the language rather than left to you.

  • Closures and late binding — the sibling family of "evaluated at a different time than you assumed" traps.

  • functools.lru_cache — the correct, bounded form of an intentional shared cache.

  • The __eq__ / __hash__ contract — where the immutability-implies-hashability link is cashed out properly.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Immutable defaults ((), frozenset(), None) — when no per-call mutable state is needed at all.

  • An explicit factory parameter — pass a callable when the construction itself must vary per caller.

🧩 Composes with

  • Sentinel objects (_MISSING = object()) — for when None is a valid value in its own right.

  • Type hints — acc: list[int] | None = None documents the sentinel pattern in the signature.

  • Linting in CI — Ruff B006 is what actually stops this reaching production.

15. Lock it in

Defaults are evaluated once, at def-time, and stored on the function.
Immutable default = shared and harmless. Mutable default = shared and permanent.

⚠️ The symmetry above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Optional: a story hook

🪝 The default list is a whiteboard bolted to the wall, not a fresh sheet per meeting.

The board goes up once, when the room is fitted out. Every meeting that does not bring its own board writes on the bolted one, so the next meeting walks in and finds last meeting's notes still there. To start clean you have to grab a new sheet at the top of your own meeting.

Bolting the board at fit-out is the default being evaluated once at def-time and stored in __defaults__. The notes still being there is mutation persisting on that one object. Grabbing a new sheet is acc = [] if acc is None else acc, running inside the body where code executes per call.
