notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The data model — Language reference: data model

  • Special method lookup — Data model: special method lookup

  • __new__ vs __init__ — Data model: object.__new__

  • functools.total_ordering — functools.total_ordering

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: Python's magic methods

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

Dunder methods usually get taught as a list — here are forty special names, memorise what each one does — and a list is exactly the wrong shape for this topic. It leaves you able to recognise __add__ without being able to answer the question an interviewer actually asks, which is why does writing a method with underscores around its name change what the + operator does?

The problem it solves shows up the first time you build a domain type — a Money, a Version, a Coordinate — and discover it prints as a hex address in every log line, compares wrong in a set, and cannot be sorted. Your object works fine as long as you only call your own methods on it, and falls apart the moment any built-in touches it.

So hold this question the whole way: when you write len(x), what does the interpreter go looking for, and where? The answer turns forty special names into one rule.

2. What Python normally does

Here is a class with nothing special in it at all.

class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents

a = Money(100)
b = Money(100)

Two objects, same value, and Python already has opinions about all of them. Ask it to show you one:

>>> a
<__main__.Money object at 0x7f3c1a2b4d90>

Ask it whether the two are equal:

>>> a == b
False

And ask it something it has no basis for answering:

>>> len(a)
TypeError: object of type 'Money' has no len()

None of that is an error on Python's part — it is the default posture, and it is a coherent one. Every object inherits from object, and object supplies exactly one answer to each question it can answer generically. For display, that is the class name and the address, because the address is the only thing it knows is true about your instance. For equality, it is identity: a == b is a is b, which is False because these are two allocations. And for length there is nothing generic to say, so it declines.

Money instance
      ↓
   type(a) = Money   ──→ your methods: __init__
      ↓  (inherits)
     object          ──→ __repr__  → "<Money object at 0x…>"
                         __eq__    → identity comparison
                         (no __len__ at all)

Notice where those answers live. They are not on the instance — they are on the type, inherited from object. And that is the thing to hold onto, because it is the whole mechanism in disguise.

So by default your object gets identity-based equality, an address-based repr, and nothing else — every richer behaviour is something the type has to supply.

3. What changes

Now the same class, with two methods added. Note that you are not calling anything or registering anywhere — you are just defining methods whose names happen to have underscores.

class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Money({self.cents})"

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Money) and self.cents == other.cents

Every one of the expressions from Section 2 now answers differently — without any of them being rewritten:

>>> a = Money(100); b = Money(100)
>>> a
Money(100)
>>> a == b
True

That is the move worth naming. repr(a) and a == b are syntax and built-ins, not method calls you control, and yet defining a method changed what they do. The names are the hook: the interpreter has a fixed table mapping each piece of syntax to a specific dunder name, and it looks that name up on your type.

And something else changed, which nobody asked for:

>>> hash(a)
TypeError: unhashable type: 'Money'
>>> {a}
TypeError: unhashable type: 'Money'

Money was hashable a moment ago, on the inherited identity hash. Defining __eq__ took that away. Python sets __hash__ = None on any class that defines __eq__ without also defining __hash__, because the inherited identity hash would now contradict your equality — two objects you have declared equal would land in different buckets, and every set and dict holding them would quietly develop missing keys. Python's position is that being unusable is better than being silently wrong.

BEFORE (object's defaults)        AFTER (you defined __eq__ + __repr__)

type slots on Money:              type slots on Money:
  tp_repr    → object's           tp_repr      → YOUR __repr__
  tp_richcmp → identity           tp_richcompare → YOUR __eq__
  tp_hash    → identity hash      tp_hash      → None  ← removed for you
  (no length slot)                (no length slot)

The trade in one sentence: implementing a protocol method buys your object a piece of built-in syntax, and the data model holds you to that protocol's other obligations whether you noticed them or not.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Conceptually, Python looks up a specially-named method. In CPython the lookup is narrower than an ordinary attribute lookup, and the difference is the source of several exam questions.

Each dunder corresponds to a type slot — a C-level function pointer on the type object. __repr__ fills tp_repr, __hash__ fills tp_hash, __eq__ and the ordering methods share tp_richcompare, __add__ fills nb_add, __len__ fills mp_length or sq_length. When you define a dunder in a class body, class creation writes your function into the matching slot. When the interpreter evaluates len(x), it does not perform an attribute lookup for "__len__" — it reads the slot on type(x) directly and calls it.

Three consequences fall out of that path, and all three are probed.

The first is that special-method lookup skips the instance entirely. Setting x.__len__ = lambda: 5 puts a key in the instance dictionary, which the slot read never consults, so len(x) still raises. Section 6 makes this visible. The reason is performance — every + in a loop would otherwise pay for a full attribute lookup — and the rule is officially "implicit special method lookup", worth naming by that phrase.

The second is the reflected-operand fallback. When x + y finds nothing usable on type(x), Python gives type(y) a turn via __radd__ before giving up. That is how 2 * your_vector can work when int has never heard of your class, and it is the standard follow-up to any operator-overloading answer.

The third is the construction split, which is the same slot mechanism one level up. Money(100) is a call on the class, so it goes to type.__call__, and that does two things in order: it calls Money.__new__(Money, 100), whose job is to allocate and return an instance, and then — only if what came back is a Money — it calls Money.__init__(instance, 100) to populate it. __new__ returns the object; __init__ must return None. Most classes never touch __new__ because object.__new__ is fine. The ones that must are immutable types, which cannot set state after allocation and so do their work during it, and singletons or interning caches, which return an existing object instead of a fresh one — and those hit the classic trap that __init__ still runs on whatever __new__ handed back, re-initialising the shared instance on every call.

5. Code / Config Example

A real value object implements a coherent protocol surface, not a scattering of dunders. Here is the hand-written form, which is what you should be able to write on a whiteboard:

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
import functools

@functools.total_ordering                    # synthesizes <=, >, >= from __eq__ + __lt__
class Money:
    __slots__ = ("cents",)                   # value objects are usually high-count

    def __init__(self, cents: int) -> None:
        self.cents = cents

    def __repr__(self) -> str:               # round-trippable: eval(repr(m)) == m
        return f"Money({self.cents})"

    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Money):
            return NotImplemented            # NOT False — lets the other type try
        return self.cents == other.cents

    def __lt__(self, other: "Money") -> bool:
        return self.cents < other.cents

    def __hash__(self) -> int:               # MUST be restored; same field as __eq__
        return hash(self.cents)

The NotImplemented return is the line most hand-written __eq__ methods get wrong. Returning False for an unknown type asserts inequality on behalf of a type you know nothing about; returning NotImplemented tells Python to ask the other operand, and only then fall back to identity. And __hash__ has to be written back explicitly, because defining __eq__ removed it.

In new code you would rarely write all that by hand. The declarative form generates the same protocol surface, correctly, in four lines:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True, order=True, slots=True)   # frozen ⇒ __hash__ is generated
class Money:                                      # order=True ⇒ all four comparisons
    cents: int

Reach for the hand-written version when the equality or ordering rule is not simply "compare the fields in order" — currency-aware money, version numbers with pre-release tags — and for everything else let the decorator do it.

6. Break it yourself

Paste this in. It attaches a dunder to an instance, which is the single fastest way to prove that special-method lookup does not go through the instance at all.

class Box:
    pass

b = Box()
b.__len__ = lambda: 5

print(b.__len__())          # ?
print(len(b))               # ?

Box.__len__ = lambda self: 7
print(len(b))               # ?

# what to look for: the explicit call works while len() does not, until the method
#                   is put on the CLASS — at which point len() starts working
# naive model would predict: len(b) is 5, because b clearly has a __len__

The explicit call prints 5. len(b) raises TypeError: object of type 'Box' has no len(). Then, after assigning to Box, len(b) prints 7 — and note it prints 7, not 5, even though the instance attribute is still sitting right there.

What that proves is that len() never looked at b. It read a slot on type(b), found it empty, and raised; once the slot was filled it used the class's function and ignored the instance's entirely. So dunders are a contract between the type and the interpreter, which is why you cannot monkey-patch operator behaviour onto one object, why Mock() needs MagicMock to fake len and __enter__, and why __getattr__ on an instance will never rescue a missing protocol method.

7. The deeper mental model

Step back and the forty special names collapse into one relationship:

      What you write              What the interpreter does

      len(x)          ─────────→  type(x) slot mp_length      → __len__
      x + y           ─────────→  type(x) slot nb_add         → __add__
      x == y          ─────────→  type(x) slot tp_richcompare → __eq__
      repr(x)         ─────────→  type(x) slot tp_repr        → __repr__
      with x:         ─────────→  type(x) slots               → __enter__/__exit__
      for i in x:     ─────────→  type(x) slot tp_iter        → __iter__
      Money(100)      ─────────→  type(Money).__call__        → __new__ + __init__
                                        ▲
                                        └── always the TYPE, never the instance

Syntax in Python is not primitive. Every operator, every built-in function, every statement form that takes an object is a thin surface over a method call dispatched on the type — which means there is no privileged set of "real" types. list is not special because the interpreter knows about lists; it is special because it fills the slots. Fill the same slots and your class is exactly as much a sequence as list is, to every piece of code that only asks for one.

That is the design decision underneath duck typing, and it is why Python's protocols are structural rather than declared. You never register a class as iterable or inherit from an interface to become one — you implement __iter__ and you are one, as far as every for loop in the language is concerned. typing.Protocol and the ABCs in collections.abc are later conveniences for talking about that fact in type checkers; they are not what makes it true.

So the honest one-line summary is not "dunders are magic methods". It is that the data model is the interpreter's published interface — a fixed list of names it will call on your type, in exchange for a fixed list of syntax it will let your objects participate in.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Where are dunders looked up? On the type, via C-level slots — the instance __dict__ is skipped entirely.
__new__ vs __init__? __new__ allocates and returns the instance; __init__ initialises it and returns None.
__repr__ vs __str__? repr = unambiguous, for developers, used in containers and tracebacks; str = readable, for users. str falls back to repr, never the reverse.
What happens if you define __eq__ alone? Python sets __hash__ = None — the class becomes unhashable.
What should __eq__ return for an unknown type? NotImplemented, not False — it lets the other operand try.
What does total_ordering need? __eq__ plus exactly one of __lt__ / __le__ / __gt__ / __ge__.
What is __radd__ for? The reflected fallback when the left operand's type can't handle the operation.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Include — the dispatch path is the concept. Re-label the Section 4 Mermaid nodes A–I and reconstruct the flow cold; the answer key is syntax → operation → slot on type(x) → dunder, with the reflected-operand branch before TypeError.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you get before the follow-up lands. Everything below Tier 1 is what they follow up with.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What's the difference between __repr__ and __str__, and which should you always define?

__repr__ is the unambiguous developer-facing form — ideally something you could paste back into code, like Money(100). __str__ is the readable user-facing form, like $1.00. The REPL echo, repr(), and anything printing a container use __repr__; print(), str() and f-string interpolation use __str__.

Always define __repr__. str() falls back to __repr__ when __str__ is missing, so one good __repr__ covers both — while the reverse is not true, and defining only __str__ leaves you reading <Money object at 0x7f…> in every traceback and log line.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Walk me through what Python actually does when it evaluates len(x), and why setting x.__len__ doesn't work.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know special-method lookup is slot-based on the type, or think dunders are ordinary attributes with decorative names.

Dunders are stored as C-level type slots on the type object — tp_repr, tp_hash, tp_richcompare, nb_add, mp_length and so on. Defining __len__ in a class body causes class creation to write that function into the length slot. Evaluating len(x) compiles to an operation that reads the slot on type(x) and calls it directly; it never performs a normal attribute lookup for the string "__len__".

That is why an instance attribute has no effect. x.__len__ = f puts a key in x.__dict__, and the slot read does not consult the instance dictionary — so len(x) still raises TypeError while x.__len__() works fine, because the explicit call is an ordinary attribute lookup. The official name for this is implicit special method lookup, and the motivation is speed: operators in hot loops would otherwise pay for a full MRO walk every time. The practical consequences are that you cannot monkey-patch protocol behaviour onto a single object, and that __getattr__ will never rescue a missing dunder.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A value object compares wrong in a set and sorts inconsistently. The team added __eq__ and __lt__ by hand. What broke?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard escalation once you have described the protocol surface — it bundles the two most common hand-rolling mistakes into one story.

Two independent failures are hiding in that description. The first is hashing: defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes Python set __hash__ = None, so putting the object in a set raises TypeError outright. If someone "fixed" that by adding a __hash__ computed from different fields than __eq__ uses, it is worse than the crash — equal objects now hash differently, land in different buckets, and set membership and dict lookups silently miss. That shows up as intermittent cache misses rather than an exception.

The second is ordering. Hand-writing only __lt__ gives you < and nothing else; >, <= and >= fall back to the inherited defaults and raise TypeError on a plain class, so comparisons behave differently depending on which operator the calling algorithm happens to use. sorted() only needs < so it looks fine, while max() with a key or a heapq operation may not.

The fix is @functools.total_ordering — define __eq__ plus one ordering method and it synthesises the other three consistently — and to restore hashing deliberately, either as __hash__ = None if the object is genuinely mutable and should not be a key, or computed from exactly the fields __eq__ compares. A frozen=True, order=True dataclass gets all of it right for free, which is the real recommendation.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

You're designing a value-object layer — money, coordinates, version numbers — used as dict keys, in sets, sorted, and serialized across services. Which dunders form the contract, and where does a naive implementation break under real use?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can specify a coherent protocol surface and its invariants, rather than recalling individual dunders.

The binding constraint is that these objects are used as keys and set members, which makes the __eq__/__hash__ contract load-bearing rather than a nicety: equal objects must hash equal, and both must be derived from fields that cannot change while the object is in a container. So I would make them immutable — @dataclass(frozen=True) — which gives a generated __hash__ over the same fields as the generated __eq__ and makes the invariant structural instead of a convention someone has to remember. Ordering comes from order=True or @total_ordering, never from a hand-written partial set. And __slots__ or slots=True, because a value-object layer is by definition high-count.

The serialization edge is where I would push back on a naive design. __repr__ should round-trip for debugging, but the wire format belongs to an explicit serializer, not to __str__ — conflating human display with a persisted format means a cosmetic change to a log line silently becomes a wire-format change, and that drift is very hard to detect. Similarly I would not overload arithmetic dunders unless the domain genuinely is arithmetic: adding two Money values is meaningful, adding two Version numbers is not, and a surprising operator costs more readability than it buys convenience.

The failure mode I would monitor first is a mutable field sneaking into the hashed state — someone adds a list of tags to the "value object", or drops frozen=True to fix a constructor annoyance. The moment that happens, every set and dict holding the object develops phantom missing keys, and it surfaces as an intermittent cache-miss rate rather than a clean crash. A test asserting the type is frozen and that hash(obj) is stable across a mutation attempt catches it in CI, which is where you want a contract violation caught.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Concern Dunder(s) Triggered by Obligation it creates
Construction __new__, __init__ Cls(...) __new__ returns the instance; __init__ returns None
Debug repr __repr__ repr(), REPL echo, containers, tracebacks should round-trip if possible
User string __str__ str(), print(), f-strings none — falls back to __repr__
Equality __eq__ (__ne__ derived) ==, !=, in removes __hash__ unless you restore it
Hashing __hash__ dict/set membership must agree with __eq__ and stay stable
Ordering __lt__ / __le__ / __gt__ / __ge__ <, sorted, min/max, heapq define all four, or one plus @total_ordering
Operators __add__ … + __radd__ … +, -, * return NotImplemented for unknown types
Container __len__, __getitem__, __iter__, __contains__ len(), x[i], for, in __getitem__ alone already makes it iterable

11. What Goes Wrong

Two different failure modes sit under this heading: wrong beliefs about how the protocol works, which produce bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "__init__ is the constructor — it creates the object."

✅ Reality: __new__ creates it, by allocating and returning the instance. __init__ only initialises an object that already exists, and must return None. The distinction is invisible until you meet an immutable type or a singleton, and then it is the whole answer.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "str() and repr() are basically the same, so defining one is enough."

✅ Reality: str falls back to repr, not the other way round. Define __repr__ first, always; add __str__ only when the user-facing form genuinely differs from the developer-facing one.

❌ Misconception: "Dunders are just methods with funny names, so I can set one on an instance."

✅ Reality: They are looked up on the type, through slots that skip the instance dictionary. x.__len__ = f changes nothing about len(x). Section 6 shows it in five lines.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

__init__ versus __new__ is a mandatory confusable and the two are genuinely different jobs: __new__ is allocation, runs first, returns the instance, and is what immutable types and singletons customise; __init__ is initialisation, runs second on whatever __new__ returned, mutates it, and returns None. Separately, do not conflate implementing a protocol with inheriting behaviour — an object gains protocol behaviour by filling type slots, which is checked structurally on the type, not by its position in a class hierarchy.

Interview Traps

  • Calling __init__ "the constructor" and stopping there — fine colloquially, but the moment you are asked about tuple subclassing or a singleton you need __new__, and not having it ready reads as surface knowledge.

  • Getting the str/repr fallback backwards — it leads directly to the wrong advice about which to define, and interviewers check it precisely because it is asymmetric.

  • Defining __eq__ and not mentioning __hash__ — the single most common data-model trap. Always address hashing in the same breath as equality, unprompted.

  • Describing operator dispatch without reflected methods — the follow-up is always "what if the left operand doesn't support it?", and __radd__ is the answer.

  • Listing dunders instead of naming the mechanism — reciting twenty special names is recall; saying "the interpreter reads a slot on the type" is understanding, and only one of them survives a follow-up.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When TO use this

  • Define __repr__ on every non-trivial class — it is four lines and it pays back on every log line, every traceback, and every debugger session for the life of the code.

  • Implement __eq__ plus __hash__ for value objects — money, coordinates, IDs, versions; anything compared by content or used as a dict key or set member.

  • Use @total_ordering or order=True when a type needs full ordering, so the four comparisons cannot drift apart.

  • Implement container protocols when the object genuinely is a container — __iter__, __len__, __getitem__, __contains__ on a type that wraps a collection, so callers can use ordinary syntax instead of learning your method names.

  • Override __new__ only for real construction control — immutable subclasses, singletons, interning caches.

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't override __new__ when __init__ would do — it is the more error-prone hook (it must return the instance, and __init__ still runs on whatever comes back, which double-initialises singletons), and it is rarely warranted.

  • Don't overload operators for cleverness — a + that means something non-obvious in your domain costs every future reader more than it saves the author. Reserve arithmetic dunders for genuine arithmetic semantics.

  • Don't hand-write a partial ordering set — __lt__ alone makes sorted() work and >= raise, which produces bugs that depend on which algorithm touches the object.

  • Don't implement __getattr__ to paper over a missing protocol — special-method lookup bypasses it entirely, so it will not help, and it will make every genuine AttributeError harder to diagnose.

  • Don't let __eq__ return False for unknown types — return NotImplemented so the other operand gets its turn; returning False asserts inequality against a type you know nothing about.

🔖 Version discipline

The data model is stable across 3.x in outline, but details move and should be stated against a version. @dataclass(slots=True) and kw_only are 3.10+. __class_getitem__ and builtin generic aliases (list[int]) are 3.9+. The set of async and number dunders has grown over releases, and __hash__ = None on __eq__ has been the rule since Python 3.0 but is a Python-3 behaviour worth naming as such. Slot names quoted here (tp_repr, nb_add) are CPython implementation detail and are not part of the language spec, so describe them as CPython rather than as Python.

13. Production Reality

The data model is how your domain objects stop being opaque blobs and become things the rest of the language, and the rest of your stack, can work with.

Why It Matters in Production

A missing __repr__ turns every log line, every traceback and every debugger frame into <Foo object at 0x7f…>, which is a tax paid on every incident for as long as the class exists — it does not cause outages, it lengthens them. A broken __eq__/__hash__ pair is worse, because it corrupts caches and deduplication sets without raising: the symptom is "the cache randomly misses" or "we processed that record twice", and it can run for months before anyone attributes it correctly.

The business framing is that the protocol surface decides whether your objects behave predictably under operations nobody explicitly wrote — sorting, set membership, logging, serialization, equality in a test assertion. Getting it right is cheap and done once per class; getting it wrong produces a class of bug that is expensive precisely because it never crashes.

Real World Usage

@dataclass and attrs are the mainstream way teams get correct __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and ordering without hand-writing them, and Pydantic builds its validation and serialization on the same protocol surface. enum.Enum uses __new__ to intern its members, which is the canonical real-world __new__. Any ORM — SQLAlchemy is the obvious one — defines __repr__ and explicit identity semantics on mapped classes so that rows are debuggable and comparable, and pathlib.Path is a good example of a stdlib type whose entire ergonomics come from operator overloading (/) plus the container and comparison protocols.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Skipped — the data model is a protocol surface rather than a benchmarkable feature, and per the no-fabrication rule no numbers beat invented ones. The one measurable claim worth making is directional: slot dispatch is a C-level function-pointer call, so it is cheaper than an attribute lookup, which is exactly why lookup skips the instance.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Slot dispatch is fast; a custom __eq__ or __hash__ written in Python runs on every comparison and every dict lookup, which is where cost accumulates.
💰 Memory Negligible — dunders live on the type, not per instance. Pair with __slots__ when instance count is high.
🧮 CPU @total_ordering's synthesized methods add one extra Python-level call versus hand-written ones; irrelevant outside tight loops.
📈 Scale A broken hash/eq contract degrades dict and set correctness, not just speed — the failure mode is silent data loss.
🔧 Maintainability Generated dunders (@dataclass, attrs) stay consistent by construction; hand-written ones are four methods that must be kept in sync forever.
🐍 CPython-specific Implicit special-method lookup and the slot table are CPython implementation details; the behaviour is specified, the mechanism is not.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • CPython object model — dunders are slots on the type, so "what is a type" comes first.

  • Names and binding — construction binds a name to whatever __new__ allocated.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • The __eq__ / __hash__ contract — the load-bearing pair, and the one with a real invariant to violate.

  • dataclasses — the declarative generator for this whole protocol surface.

  • Descriptors and the MRO — how non-dunder attribute and method lookup resolves, and where property comes from.

  • Context managers and iterators — the same slot mechanism behind with and for.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • @dataclass / attrs / NamedTuple — declarative generation instead of hand-written dunders; the default choice.

  • Plain methods — when the object needs no protocol integration, a named method beats an overloaded operator.

  • typing.Protocol — for describing a structural interface to a type checker rather than implementing one.

🧩 Composes with

  • functools.total_ordering — one comparison method plus __eq__ becomes all four.

  • __slots__ — smaller, faster value objects that still fill every protocol slot.

  • collections.abc — mixins that build the rest of a container protocol from the few methods you supply.

15. Lock it in

Syntax is a call: the interpreter reads a slot on the TYPE and dispatches to a dunder.
Define the dunder and you get the syntax — and the protocol's other obligations with it.

⚠️ The symmetry above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Optional: a story hook

🪝 __new__ builds the house; __init__ furnishes it.

Calling Money(100) first sends __new__ out to lay the foundation and hand back a bare house — the allocation. Then __init__ walks in and furnishes it, setting cents. A singleton is a __new__ that says "we already built this one, here is the key" and returns the existing house; __init__ dutifully walks in and re-furnishes it anyway, which is exactly why re-initialisation is the singleton trap.

Laying the foundation is object.__new__ reserving memory and setting the type pointer. Furnishing is __init__ writing attributes onto an object that already exists. Handing back an existing key is __new__ returning a cached instance instead of allocating — and type.__call__ calling __init__ on it regardless is the bug you have to guard against.

notes.title: The __eq__ / __hash__ Contract

headings.text: What is the __eq__/__hash__ contract, and what breaks if you violate it?
Why does defining __eq__ make a class unhashable, and how does dict lookup actually use both methods?
A team made a value object hashable by returning a constant from __hash__ to "just make it work" in a set. What's the production consequence?

You maintain a caching layer keyed on composite domain objects (tenant + resource + version). Hit rate has quietly dropped and memory is climbing. How do you reason about __eq__/__hash__ as the suspect?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • object.__hash__ — Data model: object.__hash__

  • object.__eq__ — Data model: object.__eq__

  • Hashable — Glossary: hashable

  • Hash randomization — PYTHONHASHSEED

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: Build a hash table in Python

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

Most Python rules announce themselves when you break them. This one does the opposite: violate the __eq__/__hash__ contract and nothing raises, nothing logs, and every test you wrote with two small objects passes. The container just starts giving wrong answers, and it gives them consistently enough that people build on top of them.

The problem it solves is the one behind a whole category of expensive, badly-attributed incidents: a deduplication set that keeps duplicates, a cache whose hit rate slowly decays while its memory climbs, a permissions set that "loses" a member. All three are the same bug, and none of them look like a bug in the code that does the lookup.

So carry this question through: when you ask a dict whether it has a key, what does it actually do to find out? The contract is not an arbitrary rule you have to memorise — it is the precondition that makes that procedure work, and once you have seen the procedure you cannot forget the rule.

2. What Python normally does

Start with a class that has nothing to do with hashing at all.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

a = Point(1, 2)

You never wrote a __hash__, so you might expect the next line to fail. It does not:

>>> hash(a)
8770929126234
>>> {a}
{<__main__.Point object at 0x7f8b2c0d4e50>}

Every object is hashable by default, because object supplies a __hash__ derived from the instance's identity — in CPython, from its address. And that default is quietly consistent with the other default, which is that == on a plain class also means identity. Two objects with the same values are simply two different objects:

>>> b = Point(1, 2)
>>> a == b
False
>>> hash(a) == hash(b)
False

Different objects, different hashes, and unequal. Same objects, same hash, and equal. The two defaults agree because they are both asking the same question — is this the same object? — and that agreement is exactly what makes the default safe.

Point instance ──→ object's __hash__  ──→ derived from id()
               └──→ object's __eq__    ──→ compares id()

       both answer "is it the same object?"  →  they can never disagree

So by default every object is hashable, hashing and equality both mean identity, and because they mean the same thing they cannot contradict each other.

3. What changes

Now redefine equality — the ordinary thing to do for a value object, where two points with the same coordinates should be the same point.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Point) and (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)

Equality now works the way you wanted:

>>> Point(1, 2) == Point(1, 2)
True

And hashing, which you did not touch, has stopped working entirely:

>>> hash(Point(1, 2))
TypeError: unhashable type: 'Point'
>>> {Point(1, 2)}
TypeError: unhashable type: 'Point'

That is not a bug and it is not Python being fussy. It is Python noticing that the two defaults no longer agree and refusing to let you find out the hard way. __eq__ now says these two objects are the same thing; the inherited __hash__ still says they are different, because it is built from their addresses. So Python sets __hash__ = None on any class that defines __eq__ without also defining __hash__.

It is worth seeing what it saved you from, because that is the actual subject of this note. Had the inherited hash survived, this would have happened:

>>> s = {Point(1, 2)}
>>> Point(1, 2) in s
False                       # equal to the member, and not found

An object equal to something in the set, reported as absent. Nothing raised. That is the failure this whole contract exists to prevent, and Python's judgement is that an unusable class is better than a silently wrong one.

The fix is to make the two agree again, by deriving both from the same fields:

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.x, self.y))       # the same fields __eq__ compares

DEFAULT (agreeing)              __eq__ ALONE (disagreeing)      FIXED

__eq__   → identity             __eq__   → (x, y)               __eq__   → (x, y)
__hash__ → identity             __hash__ → identity  ✗          __hash__ → (x, y)

both ask "same object?"         one asks "same value?",         both ask "same value?"
       consistent               one asks "same object?"                consistent
                                → Python disables hashing

The trade in one sentence: you may define what equality means for your type, and in exchange you take on the obligation that hashing must answer the same question.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Conceptually, a dict "looks up a key". In CPython it does two distinct things in sequence, and the contract is precisely the condition under which those two steps agree.

A dict and a set are open-addressing hash tables. To find an entry, CPython calls hash(key) and maps the result to a starting slot. Because different keys can map to the same slot, the value found there is only a candidate — so it then calls __eq__ to confirm the candidate is really the key you asked for, probing further on a mismatch.

Read the two steps and every rule about the contract falls out of them, in the right direction.

Hashing narrows; equality decides. The hash does not have to be unique — it only has to get you to the right neighbourhood. That is why the contract is one-directional: equal objects must hash equal, because otherwise the probe never visits them; unequal objects sharing a hash is a perfectly legal collision that the __eq__ step resolves. Getting that direction backwards is the most common way to show you have not thought it through.

The hash must be stable while the object is in the table. Placement happens once, at insertion. Nothing re-hashes an object because a field changed, so mutating a hashed field after insertion leaves the object physically sitting in a slot that its own new hash no longer points to. It is in the container and unreachable from it — Section 6 demonstrates exactly that.

A constant hash satisfies the contract and destroys the table. def __hash__(self): return 0 is correct: equal objects trivially hash equal. But every key lands in one probe chain, so lookup and insertion degrade from O(1) average to O(n), and building a set of N objects goes quadratic. This is the trap interviewers wait for, because the answer that "just makes it work" is the one that takes the service down at scale rather than in tests.

One CPython-specific detail matters at the system level. Hashing of str and bytes is salted per process — PYTHONHASHSEED randomises it at startup, on by default since 3.3, as a defence against collision-based denial of service. So hash("abc") differs between two workers of the same service, and any design that treats Python's hash() as a stable key across processes or across restarts is broken in a way that only shows up after a deploy.

5. Code / Config Example

The hand-written form, which is what you should be able to produce on a whiteboard, with the two failure modes sitting next to the correct one:

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
class BadKey:                                   # ❌ __eq__ alone
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __eq__(self, o): return isinstance(o, BadKey) and self.n == o.n
    # no __hash__ → Python sets __hash__ = None → TypeError at insert time
    # this is the FAIL-LOUD case, and it is the good outcome

class GoodKey:
    __slots__ = ("n",)                          # cache keys are high-count
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __eq__(self, o):
        if not isinstance(o, GoodKey):
            return NotImplemented               # let the other type try
        return self.n == o.n
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.n)                     # SAME field __eq__ compares

d = {GoodKey(1): "a"}
print(d[GoodKey(1)])                            # "a" — distinct object, equal
                                                # value, same hash → hit

In new code you would not write that by hand, because the whole risk is that the two methods drift apart over time as fields are added. The declarative form derives both from one field list, so drift is impossible:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)   # frozen ⇒ __hash__ generated from the
class CacheKey:                       # same fields as the generated __eq__,
    tenant: str                       # and mutation raises FrozenInstanceError
    resource: str
    version: int

Reach for the hand-written version only when equality is not "compare all the fields" — a case-insensitive key, a key where one field is metadata that should not affect identity. In that situation write both methods adjacent to each other with a comment saying which fields are load-bearing, because the next person to add a field is the one who breaks it.

6. Break it yourself

Paste this in. It puts a correctly-hashable object into a set and then mutates the field its hash is built from, which is the silent half of this topic — the half Python does not protect you from.

class Key:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __eq__(self, o): return isinstance(o, Key) and self.n == o.n
    def __hash__(self): return hash(self.n)

k = Key(1)
s = {k}
print(k in s)                          # ?

k.n = 2                                # mutate the hashed field
print(k in s)                          # ?
print(any(x is k for x in s))          # ?
print(len(s))                          # ?

# what to look for: the object is provably still inside the set while `in` says
#                   it is not — membership and contents disagree
# naive model would predict: `k in s` stays True, since k was never removed

The first check prints True. After the mutation, k in s prints False — while the identity scan prints True and the length is still 1. The object is in the set and the set cannot find it.

That is the whole failure mode, reproduced in eight lines and with no exception anywhere. Placement was decided at insertion using hash(1); the membership test now computes hash(2) and probes a region that was never written to. Nothing re-hashes on mutation, because nothing is watching the object. This is why "hash from immutable fields" is not a style preference — and why frozen=True is the real fix, since it turns a silent corruption into a FrozenInstanceError at the moment of the mutation.

7. The deeper mental model

Zoom out and the contract stops being a rule about two dunder methods:

   A hash table is an INDEX over an equality relation

        hash(x)  ─────→  "which shelf"      cheap, approximate, many-to-one
         x == y  ─────→  "is this it"       exact, authoritative, expensive

   the index is only valid while it agrees with the relation it indexes:

        x == y   ⟹   hash(x) == hash(y)        ← the contract
        hash(x) == hash(y)  ⟹  nothing          ← collisions are fine
        hash(x) must not change while x is indexed

Every indexed store in computing has this shape, and every one of them has the same failure mode. A database index that disagrees with its table returns rows that are not there and misses rows that are; a search index built on a stale analyser stops matching documents it contains; a sharded cache whose routing function changed loses everything written under the old one. Python's dict is a small, in-process instance of a completely general problem: an index is a performance optimisation that is only safe while it is consistent with the truth it indexes.

Seen that way, the three rules you have to remember stop being separate facts. Equal objects must hash equal, because otherwise the index disagrees with the relation. Collisions are fine, because the index is allowed to be approximate — that is what the confirmation step is for. And the hash must not change under a live entry, because an index built at write time cannot repair itself at read time.

So the honest one-line summary is not "remember to define __hash__". It is that __hash__ is an index over __eq__, and every rule in this note is the ordinary requirement that an index stay consistent with what it indexes.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The contract in one line? a == b ⟹ hash(a) == hash(b). Equal objects must hash equal.
Does the converse hold? No. Unequal objects sharing a hash is a legal collision, resolved by __eq__.
What happens if you define __eq__ alone? Python sets __hash__ = None; the class becomes unhashable and fails loud.
How does a dict use both? hash picks the probe start; __eq__ confirms the candidate at each occupied slot.
Why can't you hash a mutable field? Placement happens at insert; nothing re-hashes, so the object strands in the wrong slot.
What's wrong with return 0? Contract-correct, but all keys share one probe chain → O(n) per op, O(n²) to build.
Is hash() stable across processes? Not for str/bytes — salted per process via PYTHONHASHSEED since 3.3.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Include — the two-step lookup path is the concept. Re-label the Section 4 Mermaid nodes A–I and reconstruct it cold; the answer key is hash → probe start → occupied? → __eq__ confirm → found, with the red subgraph as what a violation does to that path.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you get before the follow-up lands. Everything below Tier 1 is what they follow up with.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What is the __eq__/__hash__ contract, and what breaks if you violate it?

The contract is that objects comparing equal must return equal hashes. The converse is not required — unequal objects may collide on hash, and that is fine, because it is resolved by an equality check.

Violate it, with equal objects hashing differently, and dict and set misbehave without raising. They locate an entry by hashing to a bucket first, so an equal object that hashes elsewhere is never visited: membership returns False for something that is in the container, and deduplication silently keeps duplicates. Nothing crashes; the data is just wrong.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Why does defining __eq__ make a class unhashable, and how does dict lookup actually use both methods?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can describe the two-step lookup, which is what makes the contract a consequence rather than a rule to memorise.

Defining __eq__ in a class body causes Python to set that class's __hash__ to None unless you define __hash__ too. The reasoning is that your custom __eq__ has almost certainly changed what equality means, so the inherited identity-based hash from object is now inconsistent with it. Rather than let you ship a silent contract violation, Python makes the class unhashable, so insertion into a dict or set raises TypeError immediately. It converts a silent data bug into a loud one at the earliest possible moment.

The lookup itself uses both methods in sequence. To find a key, CPython computes hash(key), maps it to a starting slot, and follows the probe sequence; because distinct keys can collide into the same region, each occupied slot it reaches is only a candidate, so it calls __eq__ to confirm. Hashing narrows the search to O(1) on average and equality establishes correctness — and both must be derived from the same fields, or the two steps disagree and the probe path never visits the entry you are looking for.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A team made a value object hashable by returning a constant from __hash__ to "just make it work" in a set. What's the production consequence?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard trap laid after a correct Tier 2 answer — the fix that satisfies the letter of the contract and destroys the data structure.

It is technically correct. A constant hash trivially satisfies the contract, because equal objects do return equal hashes. It is also a performance catastrophe: every object maps to the same starting slot, so the hash table degenerates into a linear probe chain. Insertion and lookup go from O(1) average to O(n), and building a set of N such objects does O(n²) work.

What makes it dangerous specifically is the shape of the degradation. At the handful of objects a unit test uses, it is invisible and fast. At production volume a deduplication pass or a membership-heavy loop silently goes quadratic, and it presents as a timeout in a piece of code that has not changed — so the investigation starts in the wrong place.

The other common variant fails in the opposite direction: hashing from a mutable field. The object is placed by its hash at insertion, someone mutates that field, and the object is now stranded in a slot its own hash no longer points to. Membership returns False for an object that is demonstrably still in the container, and nothing raises. The fix for both is the same discipline — hash from exactly the immutable fields that __eq__ compares, and make that structural by freezing the object.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

You maintain a caching layer keyed on composite domain objects (tenant + resource + version). Hit rate has quietly dropped and memory is climbing. How do you reason about __eq__/__hash__ as the suspect?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can connect a subtle contract violation to the metrics an operator actually sees.

The binding observation is that those two symptoms together are a signature, not a coincidence. A hash/eq inconsistency does not crash — it degrades in exactly this pattern, because every lookup that fails to find its prior entry is counted as a miss and inserts a fresh duplicate. So the cache grows while serving fewer hits, which is a combination that a capacity problem does not produce; a genuine capacity problem shows falling hit rate with flat or bounded memory. That asymmetry is what I would use to separate the two before touching any code.

My first hypothesis would be that the key's __hash__ and __eq__ have drifted apart — most often because someone added a field to __eq__ when the domain gained a dimension and did not add it to __hash__, or because a mutable field crept into the key and is being mutated after insertion. I would make the key an immutable value object where both are provably derived from the identical field set, which in practice means @dataclass(frozen=True) so the generation is automatic and drift is structurally impossible, and I would add a property-based test asserting that for random pairs, a == b implies hash(a) == hash(b).

For a distributed cache I would go further and stop using Python's object hashing as the key at all. hash() for str and bytes is salted per process, so two workers disagree about the hash of the same string and a restart changes it again — a cache keyed on it is not merely fragile, it is wrong across the fleet by design. The key on the wire should be an explicit canonical serialisation, versioned, hashed with something stable like hashlib.blake2b if it needs shortening.

The failure mode I would monitor first is entry count growing without a matching rise in distinct logical keys. Tracked alongside hit rate, that pair distinguishes a key-identity bug from a sizing problem in one graph, which is the difference between a one-hour investigation and a week of guessing.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Situation __eq__ __hash__ Result
Neither defined (default) identity from id() ✅ hashable; equality means identity
__eq__ only value None, set automatically ❌ unhashable — fails loud at insert
Both, same fields value value ✅ correct and usable as a key
Both, different fields value value ❌ silent dict/set corruption
__eq__ + __hash__ = 0 value constant ⚠️ correct, but O(n) per op / O(n²) build
Hashed field mutated later value value ❌ stranded entry — in says False
@dataclass(frozen=True) value (generated) value (generated) ✅ correct by construction
@dataclass(eq=True) unfrozen value (generated) None ❌ unhashable — same rule, generated

11. What Goes Wrong

Two different failure modes sit under this heading: wrong beliefs about the contract, which produce silent data bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Unequal objects must have different hashes."

✅ Reality: Only the forward direction is required — equal implies equal-hash. Unequal objects sharing a hash is a legal collision, resolved by the __eq__ confirmation step. Stating it backwards is the fastest way to show the model is shaky.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Adding __eq__ leaves hashing alone."

✅ Reality: Defining __eq__ in a class body sets __hash__ = None, making the class unhashable unless you define __hash__ too. It is the language actively protecting you, not an oversight.

❌ Misconception: "If it's hashable, it's safe to use as a key."

✅ Reality: Hashability is a property of the type; stability is a property of how you use it. A hashable object whose hashed field you mutate after insertion is stranded in the container, with no error at any point. Section 6 reproduces it in eight lines.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

Hashability is routinely conflated with immutability, and they are related without being the same thing. Immutability of the hashed fields is what makes a stable hash possible, but an object can be hashable while carrying mutable fields that are excluded from the hash, and a tuple — immutable — containing a list is unhashable. Separately, having a hash implies nothing about thread-safety or identity: it is purely about bucket placement followed by an equality confirmation.

Interview Traps

  • Stating the contract backwards — "different objects need different hashes" inverts it. Collisions are legal and expected; only equal-implies-equal-hash is required.

  • Reaching for a constant hash — it satisfies correctness and destroys performance. Interviewers specifically wait to see whether you catch the quadratic consequence unprompted.

  • Forgetting that __eq__ nulls __hash__ — and then claiming your value object "works in a set" when it would actually raise on the first insertion.

  • Assuming hash() is stable across processes — it is not, for str and bytes, and this is the detail that sinks distributed-cache designs.

  • Explaining the contract without the two-step lookup — the rule sounds arbitrary on its own. Hash picks the region, equality confirms the match is what makes it obviously necessary.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When TO use this

  • Any value object used as a dict key or set member — define __eq__ and a field-consistent __hash__ together, or let a frozen dataclass generate both.

  • Deliberate unhashability — for a mutable entity that should never be a key, leave __hash__ as the automatic None, so misuse fails loud at the insertion site rather than silently later.

  • Deduplication by value — a correct pair is the precondition for a set to actually collapse equal-but-distinct objects; without it, dedup is a no-op that looks like it worked.

  • Interning and caching of instances — where you want two equal-valued constructions to resolve to one entry.

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Never define __eq__ without making a decision about __hash__ — either supply a consistent one or accept unhashability deliberately. Papering over it with __hash__ = 0 trades a loud failure for a quadratic one.

  • Never hash from mutable fields — and note this is a usage rule, not a type rule: the class can be perfectly correct and still be misused this way. Freeze the hashed state so the mutation raises instead of corrupting.

  • Don't rely on Python's hash() as a persistent or cross-process key — str/bytes hashing is randomised per process. Use an explicit content hash (hashlib) for anything that outlives one interpreter.

  • Don't make a semantically mutable object hashable just to fit it into a set — that is solving the container's problem by breaking the object's. Use identity-based tracking (WeakSet, or keying on an ID) or insert an immutable snapshot instead.

  • Don't hand-roll the pair on a type whose fields are still in flux — the drift between the two methods is the actual production failure, and a generated pair cannot drift.

🔖 Version discipline

The automatic __hash__ = None on defining __eq__ is stable across all of Python 3.x and is a Python 3 behaviour specifically — Python 2 did not do this, which is why old material sometimes omits it. String and bytes hash randomisation via PYTHONHASHSEED has been on by default since 3.3, so never assume hash("x") is constant across runs. @dataclass(frozen=True) generating a consistent pair is 3.7+; slots=True is 3.10+. The O(1) average and O(n) degenerate complexities are properties of the hash distribution rather than of a particular release, so they do not need a version, but the CPython table implementation details do.

13. Production Reality

Hash/eq bugs are among the most expensive class of Python bug precisely because they are among the quietest.

Why It Matters in Production

None of the three standard failures crash. A deduplication set that keeps duplicates inflates every downstream cost — storage, egress, per-record processing — while reporting success. A cache keyed on a mismatched object stops hitting, so latency and memory both climb while the cache looks healthy by every metric except hit rate. A permissions or membership set that "loses" an entry grants or denies wrongly, which is a correctness failure with a compliance shape rather than an availability one.

All three pass unit tests written with two or three small objects, because the contract violation needs volume or mutation to express itself. They surface as degraded metrics rather than exceptions, which means they are often attributed to load, to a dependency, or to "the cache needing tuning" for weeks before anyone looks at the key class. Understanding the contract is what lets a team use rich value objects as keys without shipping a data-integrity bug that is hard even to attribute.

Real World Usage

Not applicable in the usual sense — this is a language-level contract rather than a product feature. Its correct implementation is what frozenset, enum members, @dataclass(frozen=True) and attrs with frozen=True all exist to guarantee, and every library offering hashable value objects is making the same promise. The most visible real-world consequence is the standard advice against using Python's hash() for sharding or cache keys across processes, which follows directly from per-process salting.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Metric Value Context Source
dict / set lookup O(1) average with a well-distributed __hash__ CPython dictobject.c / setobject.c
Degenerate (constant hash) O(n) per op, O(n²) to build every key shares one probe chain CPython open-addressing behaviour
str / bytes hash stability per-process only randomised by PYTHONHASHSEED, default on since 3.3 Python docs

⚠️ The complexities above are properties of the hash distribution rather than benchmarks — a poor __hash__ is what moves you from the first row to the second. Nothing here is a timing measurement, and none should be quoted as one.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency A well-distributed hash keeps lookups O(1); a poor or constant one degrades silently to O(n) per operation with no error to point at.
💰 Memory A broken contract inflates containers with undetected duplicates — climbing RSS with no corresponding growth in logical keys.
🧮 CPU Custom __hash__ and __eq__ are Python-level calls on every membership test; keep them cheap, and prefer hashing a tuple of primitives.
📈 Scale The failure is correctness, not speed, and it gets worse with N — more entries means more chances for a stranded or duplicated key.
🔧 Maintainability Frozen dataclasses derive both from one field list, so they cannot drift; a hand-written pair drifts the first time someone adds a field.
🐍 CPython-specific hash() for str/bytes is salted per process, so it is not portable as a persistent or cross-worker key.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • The data model / dunder protocols — __eq__ and __hash__ are slots on the type, and the auto-None rule is a data-model behaviour.

  • Mutable versus immutable — the hashed fields must be immutable for the hash to stay stable.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • dict internals — open addressing, probing and resize; how the hash is actually consumed.

  • set / frozenset internals — the same table without values.

  • dataclasses — frozen=True as the generated, drift-proof form of this contract.

  • Caching design — where the contract stops being a language rule and becomes an architecture decision.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Identity-based membership (WeakSet, keying on an ID) — when you genuinely mean "the same object", not "the same value".

  • Explicit content hashing (hashlib) — for stable, cross-process, persistable keys where hash() cannot be trusted.

🧩 Composes with

  • __slots__ — smaller hashable value objects on hot key paths.

  • @functools.total_ordering — the ordering counterpart, for keys that must also sort.

  • Property-based testing — the cheapest way to assert the contract holds for arbitrary field values.

15. Lock it in

`__hash__` is an index over `__eq__`: hash picks the region, `==` confirms the match.
Equal ⟹ same hash (required). Same hash ⟹ nothing (a legal collision).

⚠️ The symmetry above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Optional: a story hook

🪝 Hash picks the shelf; == reads the title.

A library shelves each book by a code and then confirms the exact book by reading its title. Give two identical books different codes and the librarian shelves the second one in a far aisle, then walks to the first aisle and swears the book does not exist. Move a book to a new shelf without changing the catalogue and you get the same result from the other direction.

The shelf code is __hash__, choosing the probe start. Reading the title is __eq__, confirming the candidate. Identical books getting the same code is the contract itself. And moving a shelved book is mutating a hashed field after insertion — the copy is still in the building and the catalogue can no longer find it.

You're designing an in-memory store holding 50M small records in a Python service with a tight RSS budget. Walk through whether and how __slots__ fits, and where it stops being the answer.
