📚 Reference Links

  • __slots__ — Data model: __slots__

  • sys.getsizeof — sys.getsizeof

  • Bonus — Real Python: Using __slots__ in Python

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — GeeksforGeeks: Python | Use of __slots__

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

__slots__ is one of those Python features that looks completely arbitrary until you know what Python is normally keeping inside an object. The strangeness isn't really in __slots__ at all — it's in the default you've never had to think about, because it has always just worked.

The problem it solves shows up when you have a lot of small objects. Cache entries, parsed records, graph nodes, points on a grid. Each one of them is quietly carrying a piece of machinery you are not using, and once you have a million of them, that machinery is what decides whether the worker fits in memory or gets killed.

So hold one question in your head for the whole of this note: when you write self.name = name, where does that string physically end up? Everything below is an answer to that. First Python's answer, then yours.

2. What Python normally does

Start somewhere completely ordinary — a class you have written a hundred times.

class User:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

u = User("Raje", 30)

So where did "Raje" actually go? Python put it in a dictionary, and hung that dictionary off the instance. You don't have to take my word for it — you can look straight at it:

>>> u.__dict__
{'name': 'Raje', 'age': 30}

That dictionary belongs to this one object. Every User you construct gets its own, and it is a real, separate dict sitting in memory next to the instance. Conceptually the instance is a small header plus a pointer over to that dict:

u
│
├── object header  (refcount, type pointer)
│
└── __dict__ ──→ ┌───────────────────┐
                 │ "name" → "Raje"   │
                 │ "age"  → 30       │
                 └───────────────────┘

And here is the thing that follows from that, which you have probably relied on without noticing: because it is an ordinary dictionary, nothing stops you adding to it later.

>>> u.company = "Anthropic"
>>> u.__dict__
{'name': 'Raje', 'age': 30, 'company': 'Anthropic'}

company was never mentioned in __init__. It was never declared anywhere. You just assigned it and Python accepted it, because assigning an attribute is really just putting a key in that dict. Python basically says: "Sure, throw another key into the instance dictionary."

That flexibility is not free, though, and this is the part that matters. Every single instance is paying for a whole separate hash table, and every attribute read is paying for a lookup inside it — hash the string, probe the table, come back with the value.

So by default your attributes are dynamic keys in a per-instance hash table, and that table is the thing costing you.

3. What changes

Now the same class, with exactly one line added.

class User:
    __slots__ = ("name", "age")

    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

What you have just told Python is: this class is only ever allowed these two instance attributes, and I am telling you now, at class-creation time, rather than letting you find out as you go.

Everything you actually wanted still works exactly as before:

>>> u = User("Raje", 30)
>>> u.name
'Raje'
>>> u.age
30

What stops working is the part you never explicitly asked for in the first place:

>>> u.company = "Anthropic"
AttributeError: 'User' object has no attribute 'company'

So where did the dictionary go?

It isn't there any more — and notice that it is genuinely absent rather than merely empty, which is a stronger statement:

>>> u.__dict__
AttributeError: 'User' object has no attribute '__dict__'

The values moved into the instance itself. Where there used to be a pointer off to a second object, there are now the values, sitting inline:

WITHOUT __slots__                WITH __slots__

u                                u
│                                │
├── object header                ├── object header
│                                │
└── __dict__ ──→ hash table      └── slot[0] = "Raje"
                 "name" → ...        slot[1] = 30
                 "age"  → ...
                 (and anything
                  else, forever)

There is no second object to allocate, nothing to hash on the way in or out, and — crucially — no spare room for anything you did not declare.

Why is it even called "slots"?

Because that is quite literally what the class now hands out. A fixed number of numbered storage positions, decided once when the class is created, identical for every instance of that class. Writing __slots__ = ("name", "age") is you specifying the instance layout by hand, instead of letting Python fall back on the general-purpose answer of giving every object its own dictionary.

The whole trade in one sentence: you gave up the ability to invent attributes at runtime, and you got back the dictionary's memory and its lookup on every single access.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Conceptually, the values moved inline. In CPython, the machinery that makes that work is the descriptor protocol — and it is worth seeing, because it tells you this is ordinary Python rather than a special case bolted into the interpreter.

When the class is created, each name you listed becomes a member descriptor stored on the class. Each one knows the byte offset of its value inside an instance. So the class holds the map, and the instance holds nothing but the values. You can see them:

>>> User.name
<member 'name' of 'User' objects>

That is a data descriptor, and data descriptors win during attribute lookup — which is exactly what changes the shape of a read.

Follow a read down each path and the difference is concrete. On the default class, u.name walks the type's MRO looking for a data descriptor, doesn't find one, and falls back to u.__dict__["name"] — which means hashing the string and probing the table. On the slotted class, the walk finds the member descriptor on the way down and stops there, and the descriptor goes straight to the offset. The lookup finishes earlier and does strictly less work.

Two consequences fall straight out of that design, and both are exam material. The first is that assigning an undeclared name now has nowhere at all to go — there is no slot for it and no dict to absorb it, so the only honest thing Python can do is raise. The second is subtler and catches almost everyone: the declaration belongs to one class, not to a hierarchy. A subclass that doesn't declare its own __slots__ gets a __dict__ again, and Section 6 makes that visible in six lines.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
import sys

class Point:                       # default: per-instance __dict__
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x; self.y = y

class SlotPoint:                   # fixed slots, no __dict__
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x; self.y = y

p, s = Point(1, 2), SlotPoint(1, 2)
print(hasattr(s, "__dict__"))                       # False
# s.z = 3  -> AttributeError: 'SlotPoint' object has no attribute 'z'
print(sys.getsizeof(p) + sys.getsizeof(p.__dict__)) # 152  (48 + 104)
print(sys.getsizeof(s))                             # 48   (~104 B saved)

In new code on 3.10+ you would rarely write that by hand. The dataclass form gets you the same layout with none of the ceremony, and it is what you should reach for by default:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(slots=True)             # declarative fields + slotted storage
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

6. Break it yourself

Paste this into a REPL. It takes the whole-hierarchy rule — the single most probed thing about __slots__, and the one that silently costs real money in production — and makes it visible in six lines.

class Base:
    __slots__ = ("a",)

class Child(Base):                 # note: no __slots__ declared
    pass

print(hasattr(Base(), "__dict__"))     # ?
print(hasattr(Child(), "__dict__"))    # ?
Child().whatever = 1                   # does this raise?

# what to look for: Base has no __dict__, but Child silently gets one back
# naive model would predict: both False, and the last line raises AttributeError

Base() prints False, Child() prints True, and that last assignment succeeds without complaint. Add __slots__ = () to Child and it flips straight back to False.

What that proves is worth sitting with for a second. __slots__ is not inherited as a property of the hierarchy — each class declares its own instance layout, and one class staying silent re-adds the dictionary for every instance beneath it. In a real codebase this is invisible: nothing breaks, no test fails, every feature still works. The memory saving you deployed for has simply gone, and nothing tells you.

7. The deeper mental model

Step back far enough and the specific feature dissolves into a shape you have seen before:

Normal Python object          Slotted object

class definition              class definition
      ↓                             ↓
   instance                     __slots__
      ↓                             ↓
 instance.__dict__            fixed layout, decided once
      ↓                             ↓
 any name → value             slot → value
 (decided at runtime)         (decided at class creation)

The left-hand column is Python's default posture almost everywhere, not just for attribute storage: decide late, stay open to whatever turns up, and pay for it in indirection. The right-hand column is what you get every time you let the language pin something down early instead.

Once you see it that way, __slots__ stops looking like a memory trick and starts looking like one instance of a bargain the language offers you over and over — __slots__ for attribute storage, type hints for types, frozen=True for mutability, Final for rebinding. Each one is the same deal in a different place: give up a degree of runtime freedom, and get back memory, speed, or a class of error caught early.

So the honest one-line summary is not "slots saves memory." It is that __slots__ is a layout declaration, and the memory saving is simply what falls out of having made one.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does __slots__ remove? The per-instance __dict__ (and the default __weakref__); attributes go in fixed C slots.
What is a slot, mechanically? A member descriptor on the class pointing at a fixed offset inside the instance.
Three benefits? Lower memory per instance, faster attribute access, attribute-typo protection.
The classic trap? Can't add undeclared attributes; can't weakref unless you slot __weakref__.
Inheritance gotcha? A subclass without __slots__ regains a __dict__, silently undoing the saving.
Measured saving (2-attr class, 3.10)? ~152 B dict-backed vs 48 B slotted → ~104 B saved per instance.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Include — the dict-instance-vs-slots-instance layout is the concept. Re-label the Section 4 Mermaid nodes; answer key is the Section 3 before/after pair.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you actually get before the interviewer follows up. Everything below Tier 1 is what they follow up with.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What does __slots__ do and why would you use it?

Every instance normally carries its own __dict__, so attributes are dict keys — flexible, but that's a hash table per object plus a lookup per read. __slots__ declares a fixed attribute set, and CPython stores the values inline behind class-level descriptors instead. You trade dynamic attributes for real memory savings at scale.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

How are slotted attributes actually stored and accessed, versus __dict__?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name the descriptor protocol rather than hand-waving at "it's faster".

Without slots, obj.x = 1 writes into obj.__dict__["x"], and reading obj.x does a dict lookup after the descriptor/MRO walk fails to find a data descriptor. The __dict__ is a separate hash-table object hanging off the instance, so you pay for the dict structure and for hashing on every access.

With __slots__ = ("x", "y"), the class gets one member descriptor per name, and each instance reserves a fixed C-level slot for that value inline in the object. Access resolves through the data descriptor straight to the offset — no dict, no hashing, and the lookup stops earlier in the MRO walk. Because there is no __dict__ at all, an undeclared name has nowhere to go and raises. I measured this on CPython 3.10: a two-attribute dict-backed instance totals ~152 bytes (48-byte instance plus a 104-byte __dict__), against 48 bytes slotted — about 104 bytes saved per instance, scaling linearly with instance count.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A team added __slots__ to a hot model class to save memory, and later a subclass mysteriously "still uses tons of RAM" and can be weakref'd again. What happened?

📍 Seen in the wild: the single most probed __slots__ edge case.

Two gotchas collided. First, __slots__ only removes the __dict__ if every class in the MRO declares it. The subclass omitted it, so subclass instances regained a __dict__ — the saving evaporated for exactly the type they instantiate most, and silently, because nothing breaks. Second, slotting also drops the default __weakref__ slot; if the base declared __slots__ without including it, base instances couldn't be weak-referenced, but the dict-bearing subclass can. That's why weakref "came back".

The fix is __slots__ on every class in the hierarchy — often __slots__ = () on subclasses that add no fields — and an explicit "__weakref__" entry if weak references are needed. The lesson generalises: __slots__ is a whole-hierarchy contract, not a per-class toggle.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

You're designing an in-memory store holding 50M small records in a Python service with a tight RSS budget. Walk through whether and how __slots__ fits, and where it stops being the answer.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can size the trade-off quantitatively and know when to leave pure-Python objects behind.

RSS is the binding constraint, and at 50M instances per-instance overhead dominates everything else. Removing a ~104-byte __dict__ per record — my measured figure for a two-field class on 3.10 — is roughly 5 GB, which is the difference between fitting and getting OOMKilled. So __slots__ is clearly worth it: declare the exact fields, add __weakref__ only if something actually needs it, and enforce slots across the whole hierarchy so no subclass silently reintroduces a dict.

But it has a ceiling. It shrinks per-object overhead; it does nothing about each field still being a full boxed PyObject — an int is ~28 bytes, not 8. At 50M records the bigger win is usually to stop using per-record objects at all: a columnar layout (NumPy structured arrays, Arrow, or a few parallel typed arrays) stores values unboxed and contiguously, cutting memory by another order of magnitude and improving cache locality into the bargain. So: __slots__ while the records must stay Python objects with rich methods and heterogeneous access, columnar once the data is uniform and access is bulk.

The failure mode I'd instrument first is RSS creep from an accidental __dict__. I'd assert in a test that hasattr(instance, "__dict__") is False for the hot type, so a future subclass that forgets __slots__ fails CI instead of quietly costing gigabytes.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Default (__dict__) __slots__
Attribute storage per-instance dict fixed C slots + class descriptors
Add undeclared attr? ✅ yes (dynamic) ❌ AttributeError
Memory (2 fields, 3.10) ~152 B/instance 48 B/instance
Attribute access dict lookup descriptor → slot (faster)
weakref support ✅ default ❌ unless __weakref__ slotted
Subclass without slots n/a regains __dict__ (saving lost)
Works with @dataclass? yes yes (@dataclass(slots=True), 3.10+)

11. What Goes Wrong

Two different failure modes sit under this heading: wrong beliefs about how slots work, which produce bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "__slots__ makes attribute access dramatically faster."

✅ Reality: The primary win is memory. Access is somewhat faster (descriptor → slot instead of a dict lookup), but the headline benefit is eliminating the per-instance __dict__.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Adding __slots__ to a base class makes the whole hierarchy slotted."

✅ Reality: Every class in the MRO must declare __slots__, often = (). One subclass without it reintroduces __dict__ and the saving silently vanishes. Section 6 makes this visible in six lines.

❌ Misconception: "__slots__ initialises the attributes — declaring the names is enough."

✅ Reality: It reserves storage, it assigns nothing. An instance whose __init__ never set a slot raises AttributeError when you read it. You still write the __init__.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

__slots__ gets confused with immutability and with private attributes, and it is neither. Slotted attributes are freely mutable, and slots are not access control — they restrict which names exist, not who may read or write them.

Interview Traps

  • Leading with "it's faster" — the memory saving is the real point, and overstating the speed win reads as cargo-culted.

  • Forgetting the subclass __dict__ rule — the most probed edge case; not knowing it means you can't actually deliver the saving in a real hierarchy.

  • Not mentioning the __weakref__ loss — slotting silently breaks weak references, which breaks caches and observers. A senior is expected to flag it unprompted.

  • Quoting a byte saving as universal — sizes are version- and shape-dependent. Say "measured on 3.10", not "104 bytes".

  • Saying "it's a list of allowed attributes" and stopping — that's the behaviour, not the mechanism. Member descriptors on the class, fixed offsets in the instance moves the answer up a level.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When TO use this

  • Many instances of a small, fixed-shape class — records, points, tree/graph nodes, cache entries at 10⁴–10⁸ scale, where per-instance __dict__ overhead dominates RSS.

  • When you want typo protection — a value object whose attribute set should be closed, so obj.wrongname = x raises instead of silently creating a field.

  • Hot attribute-access paths — the descriptor-to-slot path shaves the dict lookup; measurable in tight loops.

  • With dataclasses — @dataclass(slots=True) (3.10+) gets the ergonomics and the savings together.

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • For a handful of instances — the saving is per-instance, so at small counts it's noise and you've given up flexibility for nothing.

  • When you need dynamic attributes — monkey-patching, plugin attributes, and libraries that set arbitrary attributes (some ORMs, functools.wraps targets) will break.

  • Halfway down a hierarchy — a subclass without __slots__ reintroduces __dict__; and multiple inheritance with non-empty slots on both parents raises a layout conflict outright.

  • On objects that must be weak-referenceable — caches and observer patterns need "__weakref__" slotted explicitly, or they break.

🔖 Version discipline

The measured sizes (152 B vs 48 B, with a 104 B __dict__) are CPython 3.10 on this machine. Object sizes shift between releases — key-sharing dicts (PEP 412) already reduced __dict__ cost in earlier versions — so re-measure with sys.getsizeof on your target build rather than quoting these as universal. (Re-verified 19 Sep 2026 on CPython 3.9.6: identical 48 / 104 / 48 figures, so the number is stable at least across 3.9–3.10 for a two-field class.) @dataclass(slots=True) needs 3.10+. Free-threaded builds (3.13+) may alter object layout; verify before relying on exact numbers.

13. Production Reality

Memory is usually the constraint that decides how many objects fit in one worker before it gets OOMKilled, which makes this an operational decision rather than a stylistic one.

Why It Matters in Production

For services holding large numbers of small objects — cache entries, parsed records, graph nodes, ORM-ish rows — the per-instance __dict__ is pure overhead, and removing it can be the difference between running one worker and three. The typo protection is the quieter win: obj.tiemout = 5 on a dict-backed class silently creates a dead attribute and ships a bug, where a slotted class raises AttributeError on the spot. So the cost of getting __slots__ right is measured in gigabytes of RSS, plus one entire class of silent-attribute bug that stops happening.

Real World Usage

@dataclass(slots=True) is the mainstream ergonomic path and is widely used for high-count value objects; attrs offers @define(slots=True), with slots on by default. Performance-sensitive libraries slot their hot internal types, and CPython's own functools and asyncio internals do the same to trim per-object overhead. Data-heavy stacks like pandas and NumPy sidestep the question entirely with columnar storage — which is the natural next step once slots aren't enough.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Metric Value Context Source
dict-backed instance (2 fields) ~152 B (48 + 104) instance + separate __dict__ measured, CPython 3.10 (sys.getsizeof)
slotted instance (2 fields) 48 B inline slots, no __dict__ measured, CPython 3.10 (sys.getsizeof)
saving per instance ~104 B scales linearly with instance count measured, CPython 3.10

⚠️ Measured on one 3.10 build and re-verified on 3.9.6. Object sizes shift across releases and depend on field count and types — re-measure on your target interpreter before quoting.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Slightly faster attribute access (no dict lookup); meaningful only in tight loops.
💰 Memory The headline win — ~104 B/instance here, times instance count. Fields are still boxed PyObjects, so columnar layouts beat it for uniform bulk data.
🧮 CPU Fewer allocations (no per-instance dict); marginally less GC pressure.
📈 Scale Decides how many instances fit per worker — but per-field boxing caps the win at very high N.
🔧 Maintainability Closes the attribute set (typo safety) at the cost of dynamic-attribute flexibility, and complicates multiple inheritance.
🐍 CPython-specific Behaviour and sizes are CPython-specific; slots interact with __dict__, __weakref__ and MRO layout rules.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • CPython object model — an instance is a header plus attribute storage, and __dict__ is the default storage.

  • Descriptors — slots are data descriptors on the class; without this the mechanism is unreadable.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • PyObject & memory layout — how per-instance overhead accumulates at scale.

  • dataclasses — slots=True combines declarative fields with slotted storage.

  • Memory diagnosis (tracemalloc) — measuring the RSS win in practice rather than assuming it.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Columnar storage (NumPy structured arrays / Arrow) — for uniform bulk data, beats slots by unboxing.

  • Plain classes — when instance count is small and flexibility matters more than bytes.

🧩 Composes with

  • __weakref__ slot — re-enables weak references on a slotted class.

  • @dataclass(slots=True) — the common real-world combination.

15. Lock it in

`__dict__` = dynamic attribute storage, decided at runtime.
`__slots__` = fixed attribute storage, decided at class creation.

⚠️ The symmetry line above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Story hook (optional)

Slots = numbered lockers, not an open backpack.

A default instance carries an open backpack (__dict__) you can stuff anything into — flexible, heavy, and you have to rummage. __slots__ swaps it for a row of numbered lockers fixed at build time: each attribute has its own, retrieval is direct, and there's no room for undeclared junk. Hand a locker-only design to a subclass that forgets its own locker list, and it quietly straps the backpack back on.

Backpack = per-instance __dict__ · numbered lockers = slot descriptors plus inline storage · strapping it back on = a subclass missing __slots__.

notes.title: Copy Semantics (assignment vs shallow vs deep)

headings.text: What's the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?
How does deepcopy avoid infinite recursion on cyclic structures, and copy shared references correctly?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The copy module — copy — shallow and deep copy operations

  • Pickle protocol (what deepcopy reuses) — __reduce__ / __getstate__

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: Shallow vs deep copying of Python objects

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

"Copy" sounds like one operation with one meaning, and in Python it is three operations with three different blast radii. The confusion costs you the moment a structure has a second level, because the copy you made protects the outer container and shares everything inside it.

2. What Python normally does

Start with the thing most people call copying.

orig = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = orig

That is not a copy at all, and you already know why — assignment writes a pointer, so orig and b are two names for one list. Mutating anything through either is visible through both, at every level.

So you reach for the next thing up the ladder, which does make a new object:

>>> import copy
>>> sh = copy.copy(orig)
>>> sh is orig
False

A genuinely new list. Appending to sh leaves orig alone, which is exactly what you wanted. But look at what is inside the new list:

>>> sh[0] is orig[0]
True

The outer container is new; the elements in it are the same objects. copy.copy walked one level and copied the references it found, not the things they point at.

orig ──→ [ • , • ]          sh ──→ [ • , • ]
           │   │                     │   │
           ▼   ▼                     │   │
        [1,2] [3,4] ◄────────────────┴───┘

        two outer lists, one pair of inner lists

So a shallow copy is new at the top and shared underneath — and lst[:], list(lst), dict(d) and set(s) all do exactly the same thing.

3. What changes

copy.deepcopy keeps going down instead of stopping after one level.

dp = copy.deepcopy(orig)
orig[0].append(99)

>>> sh
[[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]      # shallow copy saw it
>>> dp
[[1, 2], [3, 4]]          # deep copy did not

The mutation reached sh because sh[0] is orig[0]. It could not reach dp, because deepcopy recursed the whole graph and built a new object at every level, so the two structures share nothing at all.

SHALLOW                         DEEP

orig ──→ [ •, • ]               orig ──→ [ •, • ]
sh   ──→ [ •, • ]                          ▼  ▼
           ▼  ▼                         [1,2] [3,4]
        [1,2] [3,4]
         (shared)               dp   ──→ [ •, • ]
                                           ▼  ▼
                                        [1,2] [3,4]
                                          (fresh)

What you pay for it is real. A shallow copy is O(number of top-level elements); a deep copy is O(the entire reachable graph), and it will happily duplicate a 200 MB cache that happened to be hanging off one attribute.

The trade in one sentence: you buy independence at every level, and you pay for it by copying every object reachable from the root.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

The interesting machinery is in deepcopy, because recursing a reference graph raises two problems a naive recursion cannot survive. A structure containing itself would recurse forever, and an inner object reachable by two different paths would be duplicated into two independent objects — silently changing the shape of the data.

deepcopy solves both with one device: a memo dictionary threaded through the recursion, keyed by the id() of each original object and valued by its fresh copy. Before copying anything, it checks the memo; on a hit, it returns the existing copy instead of making another.

The ordering in that last step is what makes cycles work: the copy is registered in the memo before its children are copied, so when the recursion reaches a back-reference it finds the in-progress copy and stops rather than descending again. And because the memo is keyed by identity rather than value, two paths to one object both resolve to one copy — so the copy preserves the original's sharing structure instead of flattening it into duplicates.

Immutable leaves are not copied at all. deepcopy returns ints, strings and tuples-of-immutables as-is, because there is nothing a caller could do to them that would be visible anywhere else, so the recursion terminates naturally at the bottom.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
import copy

class Session:
    def __init__(self, user, conn):
        self.user = user
        self.tags = []
        self.conn = conn                      # a DB connection — must NOT be copied

    def __deepcopy__(self, memo):             # without this, deepcopy tries to
        new = Session(self.user, self.conn)   # duplicate the connection object
        memo[id(self)] = new                  # register BEFORE recursing, or a
        new.tags = copy.deepcopy(self.tags, memo)   # cycle through tags loops
        return new                            # conn is deliberately SHARED

cfg = {"limits": {"rps": 10}, "name": "svc"}
shallow = dict(cfg)                           # same as copy.copy — inner dict shared
shallow["limits"]["rps"] = 99                 # ⚠️ this mutates cfg too
deep = copy.deepcopy(cfg)                     # fully independent

The __deepcopy__ hook is the part worth knowing for interviews: it is how you keep deepcopy usable on objects that hold something uncopyable — a connection, a socket, a lock, a thread — by deciding per-field what gets duplicated and what gets shared. The memo[id(self)] = new line before the recursion is not optional; it is the same cycle guard the module uses internally.

7. The deeper mental model

The three operations are one ladder, and the rung you need is decided by how deep the mutation you are defending against goes:

   b = a              new names        0 objects copied
   copy.copy(a)       new outer        1 level copied
   copy.deepcopy(a)   new everything   whole reachable graph copied

        depth of independence  ───────→  cost, in the same direction

There is no separate "medium copy", and that is deliberate — the language gives you the two endpoints and expects you to build anything in between by hand, which is what __deepcopy__ and a rebuilt constructor call are for. In practice most production code wants a hand-built copy that is deep in exactly one field and shallow everywhere else, and reaching straight for deepcopy is usually a sign nobody worked out which field that was.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Assignment vs shallow vs deep? Alias, no copy · new outer with shared inner · new everything, recursively.
When does shallow bite? Nested mutable members — mutating an inner object shows through both.
What does deepcopy's memo do? Maps id(original) → copy, so cycles terminate and shared refs stay shared.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Keep it to about twenty seconds out loud.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What's the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?

A shallow copy creates a new top-level object but fills it with references to the same child objects as the original. The two containers are distinct, so appending to one does not affect the other — but they share their nested contents, so mutating a nested element through either is visible through both. copy.copy, slicing, list() and dict() all do this.

A deep copy recursively copies the whole reachable object graph, so the result shares nothing with the original and mutation at any level is isolated. The cost is proportional to the entire graph rather than to the top level, and it has to handle shared and cyclic references, which it does with a memo dictionary.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

How does deepcopy avoid infinite recursion on cyclic structures, and copy shared references correctly?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand that copying a graph is a graph-traversal problem, not a field-by-field one.

deepcopy threads a memo dict through the recursion, keyed by the id() of each original object and valued by its freshly-made copy. Before copying an object it checks the memo, and on a hit it returns the existing copy rather than making a second one. Crucially, an object is registered in the memo before its children are copied — so when the recursion follows a back-reference into a cycle, it finds the in-progress copy already there and stops instead of descending forever.

The same mechanism solves the shared-reference case, which is the subtler half. If one inner object is reachable by two different paths, the memo ensures both paths resolve to the single copy, so the copy preserves the original's sharing structure rather than splitting it into two independent objects that then drift apart. Immutable leaves — ints, strings, tuples of immutables — are returned as-is rather than copied, since nothing observable depends on their identity.

10. Quick Comparison Table

b = a copy.copy(a) / a[:] / dict(a) copy.deepcopy(a)
New outer object? ❌ alias ✅ ✅
New inner objects? ❌ ❌ shared ✅ recursive
Nested mutation seen by the other? yes yes no
Handles cycles? n/a n/a ✅ via memo
Preserves shared-reference structure? n/a trivially ✅ via memo
Cost O(1) O(top level) O(whole reachable graph)
Customisation hook — __copy__ __deepcopy__(self, memo)

11. What Goes Wrong

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "copy.copy gives me an independent object I can mutate freely."

✅ Reality: Only the top level is new. Nested mutable objects are shared, so mutating them shows through both the original and the copy.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Slicing (lst[:]) or dict(d) makes a deep copy."

✅ Reality: Those are shallow copies — new outer container, same inner objects — identical to copy.copy in every nested case.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

Shallow versus deep is a mandatory confusable, and both are distinct from assignment, which copies nothing at all. The three are a ladder — alias, new outer only, new everything — and naming which rung you are on is most of the answer.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't reach for deepcopy by default — it walks the entire reachable graph, so one attribute pointing at a large cache or a parent object turns a cheap-looking call into a multi-hundred-megabyte duplication. Work out which field actually needs independence and copy that one.

  • Don't deepcopy objects holding external resources — file handles, sockets, DB connections, locks and threads do not duplicate sensibly, and copying a handle that must not be duplicated is a correctness bug rather than a performance one. Give the class a __deepcopy__ that shares them deliberately.

  • Don't assume a shallow copy protects nested state — this is the single most common copy bug: mutating a shared inner object and being surprised the "copy" changed too.

  • Don't hand-roll a deep copy of a cyclic graph — you will infinite-loop, and the memo exists precisely so you do not have to solve that yourself.

  • Don't use copying where immutability would do — a frozen dataclass with replace() gives you copy-with-changes semantics at shallow cost, and makes the aliasing question disappear instead of answering it repeatedly.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • Names, binding and assignment — assignment aliases; copying is the explicit alternative, and this note only makes sense after that one.

  • Mutable versus immutable — copies only matter for mutable nested state, since immutables are safely shared.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • The cyclic garbage collector — deepcopy's memo and the GC solve the same reference-graph traversal problem.

  • dataclasses — replace() as the value-object form of copy-with-changes.

  • Pickling and serialization — __reduce__ and __getstate__ are the same "which fields travel" question at a process boundary.

15. Lock it in

Assignment copies nothing. Shallow copies the container. Deep copies the graph.
The bug is always at the level you did not copy.

notes.title: Truthiness & Operator Protocols
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Truth value testing — Standard type hierarchy: truth value testing

  • __bool__ — Data model: object.__bool__

2. What Python normally does

if x: never asks whether x is None. It calls bool(x), and bool consults the type in a fixed order: __bool__ if the type defines it, otherwise __len__ with zero meaning false, and if neither exists the object is true. That single rule is why 0, "", [], {} and None are falsy with no special-casing anywhere in the interpreter — they are just types answering the protocol.

3. What changes

Implement __len__ on your own class and it becomes falsy when empty, for free. Define __bool__ only when truthiness and emptiness genuinely differ — a zero-balance account that still exists, a result object that is empty but successful. The same "earn the syntax by filling the slot" rule drives the neighbouring operators: in dispatches to __contains__, obj() to __call__, and a comparison or arithmetic dunder returns the NotImplemented sentinel to hand off to the other operand's reflected method before Python gives up with TypeError. The trade is that an object with a surprising __bool__ makes every if in your codebase surprising.

5. Code / Config Example

class Cart:
    def __init__(self, items): self.items = items
    def __len__(self):      return len(self.items)   # drives truthiness
    def __contains__(self, x): return x in self.items
    def __call__(self):     return sum(self.items)   # instance is callable

print(bool(Cart([10, 20])), 20 in Cart([10, 20]))    # True True
print(bool(Cart([])))                                # False — len 0

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
How does bool(obj) decide? __bool__ if defined; else __len__ (0 → False); else True by default.
What do __contains__ / __call__ power? in membership testing; making an instance callable as obj().
What is NotImplemented? The sentinel a comparison or arithmetic dunder returns to defer to the reflected operand.

15. Lock it in

`if x:` asks the object "are you empty?", not "are you None?".
`__bool__` first, `__len__` second, true by default.

notes.title: Equality, Ordering & Sorting

headings.text: Why prefer key= over a comparator function?
How does stability let you sort by multiple keys, and what actually makes Timsort stable?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Sorting HOWTO — Sorting Techniques — key, stability, cmp_to_key

  • functools.cmp_to_key — functools.cmp_to_key

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: How to use sorted() and .sort()

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

Most languages sort by handing the algorithm a two-argument comparator, so that is the shape people arrive looking for — and Python's answer is a different shape entirely. The second surprise is that Python's sort is stable and guarantees it, which turns out to be a feature you can build multi-level sorts on rather than an implementation accident.

2. What Python normally does

Sorting anything Python already understands takes no configuration at all.

>>> sorted([3, 1, 2])
[1, 2, 3]

No comparator, no key. The sort works because int implements <, and that is genuinely all sorted ever asks of an element — not ==, not a comparator, just <. You can watch it ask:

class Loud:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __lt__(self, other):
        print(f"comparing {self.n} < {other.n}")
        return self.n < other.n

sorted([Loud(2), Loud(1)])

comparing 1 < 2

One call to __lt__, and nothing else. Which also explains the failure everyone meets eventually:

>>> sorted([1, "a"])
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'

Python has no total order across unrelated types and declines to invent one, so the sort stops rather than guessing.

So sorting is built on exactly one operation — < — dispatched to the element's __lt__.

3. What changes

Now suppose the elements do not have a useful <, or you want to order by something other than the element itself. The comparator instinct says: write a function of two arguments. Python's answer is a function of one.

rows = [("eng", 90), ("sales", 90), ("eng", 70)]
sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (r[0], -r[1]))

[('eng', 90), ('eng', 70), ('sales', 90)]

key does not compare anything. It maps each element to a value that Python already knows how to order, and the sort then orders by those. That is why a tuple key gives you a multi-level sort for free — tuples compare element by element — and why -r[1] reverses one field without reversing the others.

The difference is not only ergonomic, and this is the part interviews probe:

COMPARATOR                      KEY FUNCTION

your fn runs on every           your fn runs once per element
comparison → O(N log N)         → N calls, then Timsort compares
Python-level calls              the precomputed keys natively

And a second property comes along with the sort itself. Timsort is stable — elements with equal keys keep their original relative order — and the language guarantees it rather than merely happening to provide it:

>>> sorted(["banana", "apple", "cherry", "date"], key=len)
['date', 'apple', 'banana', 'cherry']

banana and cherry both have length 6, and they come out in the order they went in.

The trade in one sentence: you give up the generality of an arbitrary comparator, and you get back N calls instead of O(N log N), plus a guaranteed stable order you can compose sorts on top of.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Two stages carry all the behaviour. The first computes every key up front — this is the decorate step, and it is why the key function's cost is paid N times regardless of how many comparisons the sort ends up doing. The second is Timsort, which finds already-ordered runs in the input and merges them; on nearly-sorted data that is close to O(n), which is the reason Timsort was chosen for a language whose users sort real-world data far more often than random data.

Stability is a consequence of two specific design choices rather than luck. Timsort only ever merges runs that are adjacent in the original sequence, and when the keys tie during a merge it always takes from the left-hand run first. Together those mean two equal elements can never swap places, which is why the guarantee can be written into the language specification rather than left as an implementation note.

That guarantee is what makes multi-pass sorting work: sort by the secondary key, then by the primary, and the stable primary pass preserves the secondary ordering within each group. The single-pass tuple key is usually clearer, but the multi-pass form is the tool when the later criterion is not known when the first sort runs.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
import functools

rows = [("eng", 90), ("sales", 90), ("eng", 70)]

# multi-level in one pass: dept ascending, salary descending
print(sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (r[0], -r[1])))
# -> [('eng', 90), ('eng', 70), ('sales', 90)]

# the -x trick only works for numbers; for text, use the stable two-pass form
by_salary = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[1], reverse=True)   # secondary first
print(sorted(by_salary, key=lambda r: r[0]))                 # then primary
# -> [('eng', 90), ('eng', 70), ('sales', 90)]   same result, any key type

# genuinely relational logic that is not expressible as a key
print(sorted([23, 11, 45, 32],
             key=functools.cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: (a % 10) - (b % 10))))
# -> [11, 32, 23, 45]

# sorted([1, "a"])  -> TypeError: '<' not supported between 'str' and 'int'

The two-pass form in the middle is the one worth remembering, because key=lambda r: (r[0], -r[1]) silently only works when the descending field is numeric. For a descending string field there is no negation trick, and stability is the answer rather than a workaround.

7. The deeper mental model

Equality and ordering look like one topic and are two, and keeping them apart resolves most of the confusion here:

   __eq__   →  "is this the same value?"    used by ==, in, dict, set
   __lt__   →  "which comes first?"          used by sorted, min, max, heapq

        a type can implement either, both, or neither
        sorting never calls __eq__ — ties are decided by stability, not equality

That is why a set is equality-comparable but unordered, why a sort can put two "equal" elements in a definite order without asking whether they are equal, and why defining __eq__ on a class does nothing whatsoever for sorted. They are separate protocols that happen to be spelled with adjacent symbols.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
key= vs a comparator? key runs once per element (N calls); cmp_to_key runs on every comparison — O(N log N).
Is sorted stable, and why? Yes — Timsort merges only adjacent runs and breaks ties leftward. It's guaranteed, not incidental.
Which dunder does sorting use? __lt__ only — never __eq__. Mixed incomparable types raise TypeError.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Keep it to about twenty seconds out loud.

Tier 1 — Verifier

Why prefer key= over a comparator function?

key= computes a comparison key for each element exactly once — N calls in total — and Timsort then compares those precomputed keys natively, in C. A two-argument comparator instead runs your Python function on every comparison, which is O(N log N) calls each crossing back into the interpreter.

It is also more expressive for the cases that actually come up: key=str.lower, key=len, key=lambda r: (r.dept, -r.salary) for a multi-level sort in one pass. cmp_to_key exists as an adapter for genuinely relational logic that cannot be expressed as a per-element value, and that is rarer than people expect.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

How does stability let you sort by multiple keys, and what actually makes Timsort stable?

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat stability as a guaranteed property you can build on, or as something that happens to be true today.

Stability means equal-keyed elements keep their original relative order, and Timsort provides it by construction rather than by accident. It only ever merges runs that are adjacent in the input, and when two keys tie during a merge it always takes from the left-hand — earlier — run first. Those two rules together make it impossible for two equal elements to swap positions, which is why the guarantee is part of the language specification for both sorted and list.sort.

That is what makes multi-pass sorting correct. To order by a primary key then a secondary one, sort by the secondary first and then by the primary; the stable primary pass preserves the secondary ordering within each primary group. The single-pass equivalent is a tuple key, which is usually clearer — but the two-pass form is the one you need when a later criterion is not known up front, or when a descending field is not numeric and so cannot be negated inside a tuple key.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Approach Calls to your function Use when
key=fn N — once per element almost always: fast and readable
tuple key N multi-level sort in one pass, ascending or numeric-descending
two stable passes N per pass multi-level where a descending field isn't numeric
cmp_to_key(cmp) O(N log N) genuinely relational comparison only
@total_ordering on the element as needed the objects themselves must be orderable everywhere

11. What Goes Wrong

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "sorted isn't stable, so I can't trust the order of equal elements."

✅ Reality: sorted and list.sort are guaranteed stable. Equal-keyed elements keep their input order, and that guarantee is the basis of multi-pass sorting.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "A comparator is the natural way to sort objects."

✅ Reality: key= is the idiomatic and faster form, because it is evaluated N times rather than O(N log N) times. cmp_to_key is a legacy adapter, not the default tool.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

Equality is orthogonal to ordering. Objects can be equality-comparable but unordered (set members), or ordered without meaningful equality. Sorting dispatches to __lt__ and never calls __eq__ — so defining __eq__ on a class does nothing for sorted, and ties are resolved by stability rather than by an equality test.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't use cmp_to_key where a key works — it reintroduces the O(N log N) Python-call cost you were avoiding, and reads worse. Reach for it only when the ordering genuinely depends on a relationship between two elements rather than on a property of one.

  • Don't sort mixed or incomparable types — sorted([1, "a"]) raises rather than guessing an order. Normalise the types first, or supply a key that maps everything into one orderable space.

  • Don't hand-write a partial comparison set on your element — defining only __lt__ makes sorted work while >= raises, so correctness depends on which algorithm happens to touch the object. Use @total_ordering, or sidestep it with key=.

  • Don't re-sort repeatedly to maintain order — if the collection needs to stay ordered as it changes, that is heapq, bisect.insort, or sortedcontainers; repeated sorted calls turn an O(log n) insert into an O(n log n) one.

  • Don't sort when you only need the extremes — min, max, and heapq.nlargest(k, …) are O(n) or O(n log k); a full sort to take the top three is wasted work that grows with the data.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • The data model / dunder protocols — sorting dispatches to __lt__, and @total_ordering is how you fill in the rest.

  • Equality and identity — ordering uses <, which is a different protocol from == and from is.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • list internals and Timsort — run detection, galloping merges, and the near-O(n) behaviour on partially sorted input.

  • heapq and priority queues — maintaining order incrementally instead of re-sorting.

  • bisect — binary search and ordered insertion over an already-sorted list.

15. Lock it in

Sorting asks one question — `<` — and asks it of a key you computed once per element.
Stable means ties keep their input order, which is what lets you sort in passes.
